Season's composer, three defects the five add chips were hiding, and a measurement that had been inflating itself¶

The in-page composer replaces a select and three bare inputs. It sits directly above the Track it is adding to, because the thing you are describing and the picture of where it lands belong on screen together — a drawer covers the Track, which means composing a date range while unable to see the range. 🔴 And the form follows the record: a draw asks for one date, an event asks for a window. Not a union of every type's fields with the irrelevant ones greyed out, which is how a form starts lying about what the record holds.

🔴 A DATE PICKER, IN A PORTAL FOR A BOT THAT HAS UNDERSTOOD "in 3 weeks" FOR A YEAR. chrono-node is already a dependency and parseAdminDate() is already how every admin date reaches this database. The composer takes anything a person would type and echoes what it resolved to, in words, under the field. ⚠️ The parsing happens on the SERVER, through a new /api/parse-date that calls the bot's own parser — shipping a second parser to the browser would put two implementations behind one promise, and the day they disagreed the echo would be a lie about the thing being saved. parseAdminDate has a documented timezone subtlety of its own ({ timezone: 0 }, so the host clock cannot shift a date across a day boundary) that a browser reimplementation would have to reproduce correctly, forever, somewhere nobody would think to check.

🔴 THE FIVE ADD CHIPS ALL DID THE SAME THING. Each passed its own key to onAdd, and every call site threw it away with () => setShowAdd(true) — so clicking Playlist and clicking Draw opened an identical form defaulted to Draw. Five controls, one behaviour, and the only way to notice was to click two of them and compare.

🔴 AND THE PATCH-NOTE CHIP STAGED A CALENDAR EVENT. patchnote was not in KIND_TO_ENTITY, so it fell past the draw branch into the calendar one and produced calendar.add with category:'Event' — a patch note quietly filed as an event, under a control labelled "Patch note". It stages patchnote.addSeason now, with that op's own payload keys rather than the calendar's: resolveReleaseDate() reads releaseDate, so sending endDate would have parsed an empty string.

🔴 npm run portal:coverage HAD BEEN INFLATING ITS OWN NUMBERS, and today's commit is what exposed it. Each realm's "have" set was the ENTIRE portal's class vocabulary, so the per-realm file list it was unioned with could not change a single result — a class emitted only by Season counted as covered on Broadcast. Adding the composer moved five realms that do not render it, 51% to 57% in one commit, which is not a thing a Season-only surface can do. The portal side is scoped the way the mockup side always was now: shared chrome plus the realm's own modules. The honest figure is 53%, and every realm dropped between one and eight points. ⚠️ Every coverage number quoted before this commit was high by roughly that much.

⚠️ Two more instrument faults, both mine, both in the same hour. The stub matched its route regexes against the raw path including the query string — every regex here is $-anchored, so /api/parse-date?q=… fell through to the unrouted {ok:true} branch and the composer's echo read "not a date yet" for every value, which looks exactly like a parser that cannot parse. It matches on the pathname now, as a server does. ⚠️ portalHarness.test.js could not have caught it: that gate compares the keys a stub returns against the keys the real route promises, and a route whose regex never matches still has the right keys. And a scripted multi-edit helper printed a ✓ per edit before writing the file, so an assertion failing on a later edit silently discarded the earlier ones that had already been reported as done — two changes were confirmed in the transcript and absent from the file.

The Track gets a window you can move¶

🔴 A FIXED WINDOW CANNOT BE WRONG, ONLY USELESS. seasonWindow() spans everything the season holds — six to ten weeks for a real CODM season — so fourteen draws and twenty-three calendar items shared one axis and the single-day ones (eleven of the fourteen) computed to under two pixels each. The plot was complete and unreadable. It now zooms and pans: a zoomer in the panel header beside the view tabs, and an overview scrubber above the plot showing every item in the season at once with the visible window drawn over it — drag the middle to pan, drag either end to resize.

The window is state, and null means fit. Keeping "fitted" as an absence rather than a copy of the fit window means the plot re-fits when the season's own extent changes: staging a draw three weeks past the battle pass widens the axis, instead of leaving the new bar outside a window that was correct when it was captured.

⚠️ Every window is clamped in one place, so the three ways to move it — buttons, drag, and the fit reset — cannot disagree about where the edges are. A window that fits is slid back inside rather than narrowed (losing days on a pan is the kind of quiet wrongness nobody reports, because the picture still looks plausible), a window wider than the season becomes the season, and zooming in stops at a three-day floor because barGeometry divides by the span. The readout says "27 days shown" rather than a zoom level: one is a fact about the picture, the other about the control.

🔴 THE SCRUBBER'S FIRST VERSION WAS ONE STRIPE. .scrub .mini is absolutely positioned with no top, so all thirty-seven items stacked at the same y and the overview showed that the season has things in it and nothing else. One row per lane now — the adopted stylesheet's own comment calls this strip a filmstrip, and a filmstrip has frames.

And tools finally has a caller. It was one of two Shell props nothing passed, filed as dead code; it is the panel-header slot beside the view tabs, which is exactly where the adopted design puts the zoom control.

⚠️ left_click_drag does not exercise this, which is worth writing down: it synthesizes mouse events, and the handlers listen for pointer events so that setPointerCapture can keep a drag alive when the pointer leaves the strip — which every drag to an edge does. Verified with real PointerEvents instead: pan moved the box 18.2% → 4.5% at constant width, and the right handle took the window 27 days → 20.

Repairs, and a defect predicate that was wrong twice before it was asked about¶

Season gets a third view. 🔴 TWO OF THE THREE DEFECT FINDERS HAD NO CALLER ANYWHERE. findOverlaps and findGaps are exported from track.logic.js, one of them documented in its own comment as "the third defect the Track exists to surface", and nothing read either — so the Track had been surfacing exactly one kind of finding while two more were computed, tested and thrown away.

🔴 AND THE MOMENT ONE WAS READ, IT TURNED OUT TO BE BROKEN. findOverlaps calls laneFor(item), which read item.kind — and the Track's own items carry lane and no kind at all, so every item fell through to the 'event' default and the finder saw one lane containing the entire season: 61 overlaps across 37 items, including a playlist "overlapping" a draw. A pure function with no reader cannot be wrong in a way anybody sees.

🔴 THEN THE FIXED VERSION WAS STILL WRONG, FOR A DIFFERENT REASON. Scoping overlap to lanes where concurrency should be impossible sounded right and gave 47 findings — every one a pair of playlists, and CODM plainly runs many playlists at once (seven are live on the same days in the real data). Two premises, both plausible before they were run, both describing ordinary scheduling. A third guess would have been a guess, so it was put to Harkirat with the two measurements attached rather than tuned again. His answer: the flaggable case is the same thing entered twice — a title repeated over days that overlap, which is a mistake rather than a schedule. 17 findings, four of them real double entries in the live data.

⚠️ Containment with a length floor, deliberately not fuzzy distance. Exact-after-normalising catches punctuation and case; containment catches "Undead Legion Series Armory" inside "Undead Legion Series Armory Draw"; the eight-character floor is what stops containment matching every fragment of every title. "Week 2" and "Week 3" differ by one character and are consecutive playlists — precisely the case a distance metric gets wrong, which is why there is no distance metric.

⚠️ A clean group is still drawn, dashed and dimmed. "No duplicates" is a different statement from "we did not look", and a list that shows only problems cannot tell you which it is.

⚠️ Repairs reads the VISIBLE window, not the whole season, because findGaps is defined against a window — a gap is a stretch of the axis you are looking at with nothing in it. Zooming therefore changes what Repairs reports, which is honest; the alternative is a gap count that quietly means something other than the picture beside it.

⚠️ The backtick-in-a-template trap fired for the ninth time, in the comment recording why the overlap group was removed. Caught at node --check this time, because an odd count fails loudly — it is the even counts that ship.

The routes get executed, and the first run finds an empty diff on the review screen¶

scripts/portalRoutes.test.js calls the handlers. Nothing in this suite ever had: portalApi is a source scan for requireAdmin, the rest test pure functions, and portalHarness compares the stub's keys against the routes' promised keys without ever sending a request. It runs handlers straight out of ROUTES rather than over HTTP — no listener, no port collision, and no chance of hitting a portal somebody else is running. ⚠️ The refusal cases run everywhere, always (sessionFor returns null on a missing cookie before it queries), and the 200 cases skip loudly without a local database.

🔴 AND IT FOUND A SILENT-WRONG-RESULT BUG IN ITS FIRST RUN. previewSet reproduced the exact || defect that validateSet, twenty lines above it, had already been fixed for — under a comment explaining the hazard at length. Most entities' validate() returns only { payload }, so handing the bare result to preview() drops target, and draw.edit's preview threw on op.target.category. /api/review catches preview failures and still answers 200, so every staged draw.edit had been rendering an empty diff on the review screen — the one screen whose entire job is showing what is about to change. A fix that lands in one function and not its neighbour is how a defect survives being fixed.

⚠️ The test skipped itself the first time, and the reason is worth knowing. require('portal/server') pulls in modules that call dotenv against the production .env, and dotenv does not overwrite a variable that is already set — so a later config({ path: '.env.dev' }) is a no-op and process.env.MONGODB_URI is the live Atlas URI. It read prod's URI, saw it was not local, and stood down on a machine with a perfectly good mongod running. It parses .env.dev itself now, which also makes the local-only guard absolute.

The Board moved onto the adopted classes — .bbar, .bcols, .bcol with a real header, .bcard with the realm's accent. 🔴 And the card stopped being a <button>, because it contains buttons. A button inside a button is invalid HTML and the browser does not error: it closes the outer one early and reparents what follows, so the card's own click target silently stopped covering its own content. It had been that way through the .card version too. Gated now, with a falsifier. ⚠️ The column note moved into the header: it used to sit under the cards, so a column with six of them put its own explanation a screenful below the thing it explains — the affordance-distance shape again.

⚠️ The backtick-in-a-comment trap fired for the tenth and eleventh times in one hour, one of them inside the comment recording the previous one. The build refuses to emit a file with a backtick in an HTML comment now — the source-level check existed but ran at the END of the suite, so a broken build got as far as four failing render cases whose message named a variable nobody wrote (sum is not defined, from a comment that said .bcol-sum).

Paste a list, and compare two builds¶

The composer takes a pasted list, parsed as you type, with what it understood shown before anything is staged. 🔴 The parsing is the BOT'S OWN, over HTTP — parseBulkDrawList and parseBulkEvents in utils/adminParser.js are what /manage has ingested pasted lists with since it was built, including every trap already paid for there: a date written "July 16, 2026" splits across two comma fields and has to be rejoined, a bulleted paste out of Notes arrives as one physical line and has to be scanned per line or the last entry swallows everything after it. A browser reimplementation would preview rows the bot then reads differently, which is the one thing a preview must not do.

🔴 A LINE THE PARSER CANNOT READ IS SHOWN, NEVER DROPPED, and the count says both numbers — "2 of 3 lines understood". A paste where three of eight lines fell out silently is exactly the failure a preview exists to prevent. ⚠️ The fixture stub failed that case first, which is worth recording: Date.parse("with no date 2026 UTC") returns January 1st, so a nonsense line came back understood with a date nobody typed. The stub now requires a candidate to look like a date before offering it to the parser, and the real route has a case of its own in portalRoutes.test.js.

A pasted list stages as ONE changeset, not one per line. Eight pasted draws as eight changesets would fill the Review screen with eight separate transactions to commit and discard individually, which is not what somebody who pasted one list means.

Armory gets Compare — two or three builds side by side, their real Discord cards above a field-by-field table. 🔴 It answers the question the coverage flag cannot: near-duplicate tells you two builds share a gunsmith code and cannot tell you which to keep, and deciding meant opening two rows in turn and holding the first in your head. ⚠️ Rows that AGREE are drawn too — showing only the differences would be shorter and would answer a different question, because "identical apart from the image" is a conclusion you can only reach by seeing the fields that match.

⚠️ And the harness answered every preview request with the same card. Invisible on the one-row preview panel — one card, one selection, nothing to compare it to — and obvious the instant Compare put two side by side: two chips reading .50 GS above two cards both reading AK-47. A stub that answers the same thing to every question cannot demonstrate the feature it stands in for.

The build editor, and the whitespace trap running the other way¶

🔴 EDITING A BUILD MEANT CLICKING ONE TABLE CELL AT A TIME, AND EVERY CELL WAS ITS OWN STAGED CHANGE. Five attachments, a badge and an image key is seven separate edits through the Manifest — seven changesets, seven rows on the Review screen, for one act. The editor is the surface /manage's modal has always had and the portal did not: the whole record at once, staged as a single loadout.edit. Identity with the derived weaponKey shown read-only, the gunsmith code with a Copy control and disabled on DMZ (where the card omits it), attachments as removable rows, badges, the rank field in the vocabulary adminParser validates, and the image.

⚠️ The preview moved INSIDE it, which retires the standalone LIVE PREVIEW panel. That panel showed the card for whichever row you last clicked, beside a table you were not editing — a preview with nothing to preview against. Card and fields are one screen now, which is what .bed-side is for.

⚠️ The image URL is built by the bot's own helper, over the wire. buildImageUrl in utils/loadoutRender.js is the one place that knows the convention — a bare key becomes a Cloudinary path with f_auto,q_auto baked in, and a value that is already a full URL passes through untouched (two LOCUS rows imported from imgur still depend on that). A client-side copy would hardcode the cloud name and become the second home of a transform convention utils/cloudinaryDeliveryUrl.js exists to keep in one place.

🔴 AND THE htm WHITESPACE TRAP RUNS BOTH WAYS. The existing gate catches a line ending in a WORD before an inline tag; htm drops the whitespace on both sides of a line break, so a line ending in a closing } before a line starting with prose loses the space too — "most builds carry 5.Slot labels are only ever filled by", rendered, in a file the first gate had already passed. ⚠️ The first version of the new gate was too noisy to keep: it listed known attribute names to skip, a list needing maintenance forever and already wrong inside one file. The discriminator is the SHAPE — an attribute value is name=${…} and the whitespace between two attributes means nothing, while a prose interpolation never carries that = — plus a JS-keyword filter, because } closing a block before const … is ordinary code. A gate with false positives gets suppressed rather than obeyed, so it ships with a falsifier proving all four cases.

Armory 50% → 57%, overall 61%.

Analytics stops quoting the Discord command and starts measuring¶

🔴 The lowest realm at 54%, and the gap was never styling. Usage and Timing rendered the /bot analytics text exports inside <pre> blocks — the Discord command's own downloadable .txt, pasted into a web page — while 06-access-and-analytics.html specifies five views of structured data. Two different programs, not one under-styled version of the other.

The route already computed everything and was throwing most of it away. computeUsageStats/computeTimingStats gained three additive things and no new query: an ok and a bg accumulator inside the byCommand $group already running, an ack-distribution $bucket beside the two percentiles, and a caller-supplied limit whose default is the Discord panel's own number, so the portal can ask for depth without lengthening the text export in Discord.

Reach and Search are new, and neither duplicates a Discord number — /bot analytics has five pages and neither exists there. context and installType are written on every event by utils/eventStore.js and had never once been read back; they are the measurement the whole v3 guild-install line exists to answer. And a search term that returned nothing is the only figure in the system describing what somebody WANTED rather than what the bot did.

⚠️ Deleting the layer being replaced is part of the change, not a follow-up. The three text exports are gone from the payload along with the three builds per page load. Their facts were not lost: eventRiver already fetched whole AlertLog documents and discarded level and detail, so level is a filter now and detail is searchable — which composes with the kind filter in a way prose never did.

Five defects the gates could not see, all found by opening the page. ⓵ The harness stubbed usageStats/timingStats as fixture arrays where the route returns objects — the exact defect portalHarness.test.js's own header describes, committed a second time in the same function, on the two fields nothing was reading yet; the old component touched only usageStats.current, undefined on an array, so a header silently did not render and every gate stayed green. That test checks shape now, not just key presence, with its own falsifier. ⓶ Per-command shares summed past 100% because the stub folded admin commands into byCommand while taking current from the product-only total — production cannot produce that, so the harness was teaching a defect the code does not have. ⓷ The dependency bars painted their leader orange by construction: a fault colour keyed off "more than half the top" fires on the top row whatever the numbers are, the same shape as the success-rate tile that was orange at 99%. A weekly TOTAL is not a speed at all — 52ms across 447 calls versus 3.6s across one — so the colour comes from the per-call average and the row states it. ⓸ The busiest rows are background jobs, and prefixing every row with a slash asserted that /webp_nameplate is a command a person can run. ⓹ The Outcomes paragraph named the four outcomes that had never fired — a comment about a snapshot, stale the first time one does. It is computed now.

⚠️ And two in ?empty=1, the flag whose entire job is catching this. alertStats, outcomeStats, entryStats and ackBuckets are arrays, the zeroing pass skips arrays, and three of them were listed there anyway — so naming them read as coverage while doing nothing. An empty portal showed "ERRORS 24H 23" and a sparkline reading 3 2 4 3 2 4 4 beside a river saying nothing had ever been recorded.

Analytics 54% → 75%.

The portal could not say that anything had gone wrong¶

🔴 Every realm was fetchJson(path).then(setData) with no catch, and fetchJson called res.json() on whatever came back. So a 500 (an HTML error page), a dropped connection and an expired session all produced a rejected promise nobody handled, and the page sat on the word "Loading" for as long as anyone was willing to look at it. Of the design's six async states — skeleton, refreshing, slow, failure, progress, page banner — exactly one existed, and it was the word Loading in an inline style.

⚠️ Neither instrument could see it. portal:orphans asks whether a class has a rule, and every one of these had one, sitting unused. portal:coverage counts the shared shell against all eight realms at once, so an entire missing subsystem read as a small diffuse gap spread across eight numbers rather than as one absence. Attributing async.js to the shared set the way the mockup attributes Shell.async moved the measurement 64% → 70%, every realm lifted — which is what the gap was actually worth.

fetchJson always resolves now, and the hard part was what NOT to convert. The commit path reads a 409 carrying the gate result {ok:false, reason}, and Access reads a 400 carrying {error}. Collapsing every non-2xx into a generic failure would have silently destroyed both — the caller would show its fallback string and the specific sentence the server wrote would be gone. Only 5xx, an unreadable body and a connection that never landed are converted; everything else passes through with httpStatus added. scripts/portalAsync.test.js exists for that distinction.

Six things the build surfaced. ⓵ The BOOT had no states at all, and it is the request every other one waits behind — app.js awaited /auth/csrf and rendered nothing until it answered. Worse after the change than before: an unguarded fall-through would render a realm with session set to a failure object, so every csrfToken in the app would be undefined and nothing could be saved, by a portal that looked completely normal. ⓶ Review's commitAll looped over changesets, awaited each, and threw every answer away — a tier-3 changeset refused for a mistyped confirmation word produced no message and a list that refreshed looking identical, and it kept going after a refusal, which is the opposite of what committing in order is FOR. ⓷ Armory's builds defaulted to [], so the first frame of every visit was a complete, confident, empty Armory — "0 builds · 0 weapons · 0 flagged" over an empty rack. An empty state and an unanswered request must never look alike. ⓸ Discard answers {state:'discarded'} with no ok key, so the obvious refusal test would call every successful discard a failure. ⓹ The boot frame was wrapped in .app, a grid sized for a header and a rail that do not exist yet at boot — the whole state rendered as a 30-pixel sliver in the corner, correct markup and invisible result. ⓺ Rendering the banner AND the failbox said the same two sentences twice.

⚠️ Every state is reachable from the address bar — ?fail=500, ?fail=/api/season, ?fail=offline, ?fail=garbage, ?fail=expired, ?slow=4000 — because a state nothing can put on screen is a state nobody designs and no check can open.

Seven irreversible operations existed and none could be reached¶

🔴 core/ops declares seven tier-3 operations and the portal offered none of them. utils/adminAccess.js has a whole permission built for them — destructive, deliberately excluded from all so the owner typing "all" is not quietly handing somebody the right to purge the season, grantable only by the owner, enumerated by name in every permission summary — and review.logic.js has the commit gate that refuses an unexported one. The button was never built. An owner could grant somebody the Destructive permission and neither of them could find a single thing to do with it. No gate could see that, because every gate here measures what the code DOES and a capability with no affordance does nothing; the conservation check now added reads the registry and fails when a tier-3 op has no row.

🔴 AND THE EXPORT IT IS GATED ON EXPORTED NOTHING. POST /api/changeset/:id/export set exportedAt = new Date() and returned the timestamp — no file, no rows. So the interlock the entire tier-3 design rests on was satisfied by pressing a button that produced nothing, while the confirmation told the reader their export was "the only way back" from a purge. There was no way back. A gate that cannot fail is bad; a gate that manufactures a false assurance about irreversible data loss is worse. It returns the changeset's baseline now — the real records — and the client saves the file; a changeset staged before that field existed is refused rather than marked satisfied over an empty payload.

⚠️ Review named the blocker and offered no way through it — "1 tier-3 change needs an export before it will commit", with the only Export control one realm away on Season's Board and nothing saying so. A blocker that states a precondition without the control that satisfies it is a dead end with good manners.

Every row is present, legible and disabled with the reason for an admin who lacks the permission. Hiding them would teach nothing, produce a support question, and conceal from that person that somebody else can do this to their data. ?destroy=1 in the harness renders the state the mockup could not: a non-owner who holds the permission, which is the case the confirmation's last sentence is written for.

⚠️ The strip stages; it does not purge. The mockup gates the button on a session-scoped export, which here would be a second export concept gating nothing real — the export is a property of a changeset, and the changeset does not exist until the op is staged. The interlock sits one screen later where it is genuine, and every row says so.

The portal could promote a draft it had no way to create¶

🔴 Five draft operations exist in core/ops; /manage reaches all five and the portal reached none — so the promote row added to the one-way strip was an action on a thing nobody could make. Season now has the draft zone: start one from a title, see what is staged in it and how many items, and discard it. Promote stays in the one-way strip, because it is the one draft operation that cannot be taken back — and the bar says so, since a reader who has staged a draft and cannot find the button concludes the feature is unfinished rather than that it is somewhere safer.

⚠️ /api/season destructures draft OUT of live, and the first version of the promote row read live.draft — always undefined, so it said "No draft is active" over an active draft, permanently. The test passed, because its fixture put draft on live: a fixture that agrees with the code instead of with the API proves only that the code agrees with itself. It asserts the route's shape now. The same defect ran the other way in the harness, whose FIX.draft is a real active: false subdocument that a first pass force-activated — so the draft bar rendered "untitled · 0 items" on every load.

🔴 AND THE IDENTITY EDITOR HAD BEEN WRITING NOTHING, SILENTLY, ON EVERY FIELD. season.setTitlesDeadlines reads Discord's modal format — mainTitle, bpLine, rankLine, dmzLine, one line per deadline — and the portal composes discrete fields, because a web form has three inputs where a modal has one textarea. It sent currentSeasonTitle / bpTitle / bpEnd / bpEndTBD straight through, so every line read as undefined, applyLine returned the current values unchanged for all three, and (op.payload.mainTitle || '') fell back to the existing title. The op validated, the changeset staged, Review displayed it, committing it wrote exactly nothing, and every surface reported success. Nothing could catch it: validate() is a pass-through, preview() read the same key apply() did and so agreed with the no-op, and every test in seasonOps.test.js reaches validate() and invert() only — because apply() needs a Mongo session. The fix is additive and the line path is untouched, so Discord behaves identically; applyFields is exported for the one seam that is testable without a database, and the falsifier asserts an unknown key is not silently absorbed as a rename.

⚠️ editingDraft was a prop the caller hardcoded to false — it reached SeasonRecord, which styles the summary strip for it, and nothing could ever set it. The whole draft half of that component was built, styled and unreachable. The Live/Next switch is the mockup's own: one editor, two seasons, said out loud rather than inferred. Calendar banners are absent in the Next scope, because calendar.setBanners writes the live document and has no draft equivalent — guarding only the save left three inputs on screen that accepted a URL and dropped it, the same silent no-op re-introduced two lines from its fix. And pasting into the draft replaces that list rather than adding to it (the draft bulk ops $set the whole array, which is what the modal's textarea means), so the confirmation says which of the two operations is about to run — a toast afterwards saying "replaced" tells somebody what they have already lost.

Coverage 61% → 71%, orphans 0. ⚠️ The instrument was corrected too: its per-realm file lists were hand-maintained and Access's had gone stale, counting every class the SelectionBar emits as missing from a realm that plainly renders one. It follows the import graph now, which cannot go stale because it is the code.

Eighteen of forty-two declared operations had no way to run them¶

🔴 The previous pass found three subsystems that were built, permissioned, tested and unreachable. This one asked how many more there were, and counted. core/ops declares 42 operation types; 18 were named by no portal source file at all. The check that found them is the only shape that can see a thing which is not there — count what one authority declares against what another offers — and it is now a gate, scripts/portalOpsReach.test.js, which every op must pass or carry an entry saying why there must not be a button for it.

⚠️ An excuse on that list is a claim that gets checked, not a suppression. Five ops are excused as inverse-only — produced by another op's invert() and by nothing else — and the gate asserts both halves of that: no /manage action id (the property that makes an op unpickable) and a real inverting producer somewhere in core/ops. Eight more are excused as reached through an equivalent op, and the gate asserts the named equivalent is itself reachable, because an excuse that points at a second absence is not an excuse. Each claim ships with a falsifier.

loadout.bulkAdd and loadout.bulkReplace were the two that mattered. Tier 2, real action ids (loadouts_mp:bulkadd), a permission scope, a tested apply() with a compound inverse — and no affordance anywhere. The Add form does one build at a time, and a build is a weapon, a category, five attachments, a code, an image and its badges; retyping forty of those is exactly what the paste box exists to avoid. Armory has a Bulk view now: paste, preview, stage, and an export that emits the same grammar the paste box accepts.

🔴 The mode is a control, not a parsed field. In Discord the mode comes from which page you opened, and upsertBulkBlocks applies it to every block unconditionally — the format dropped its Mode segment on 2026-08-22. The portal shows MP and DMZ on one screen, so the thing Discord gets from context has to be stated: a paste that means DMZ and lands in MP is a silent wrong result, and the switch is the only place that decision is visible. Add and Replace are one upsert and the card says so rather than offering two buttons that do one thing.

⚠️ The preview counts what was actually lost, which is not the length of the error array. parseBulkLoadoutList pushes an error and drops the block when it cannot read the header, and pushes an error but keeps the block when a badge token is unrecognised — so "6 problems" over a paste where four builds saved fine is both alarming and wrong. The route returns the block count, which makes the split exact: rejected = blocks − parsed, warnings = errors − rejected. That decomposition is derived from the parser's own control flow and asserted against the real parser, on text built to produce one of each, so a change there fails a test rather than silently re-conflating the two.

A scopeless export is a refusal now, not an empty file. /api/armory/export answered 200 with an empty string for a request naming nothing — which reads as "there was nothing to export" rather than "you did not say what to export", and those are very different when the file is the stated way back from a purge.

The portal could publish a patch note and purge every one, and nothing in between¶

🔴 Four more of the eighteen: patchnote.setDateInfo, setUrls1, setUrls2 and editSeason. A typo in a published season title was fixable only from Discord. Season has the record panel now — every published entry on one spine, newest first, the current one filled and the rest outlines — and an editor behind each row. The current entry and a past one take different ops, which is the bot's own split rather than a simplification: /manage edits the newest through three separate actions (date/info, images 1–5, images 6–10) and a past one through a single editSeason. Following that means a change made here reads on Review exactly as the same change made in Discord would.

🔴 The release date could have moved without anybody touching it. setDateInfo sets releaseDate on every call, and parseReleaseDateTime returns new Date() for anything it cannot read — including an empty string, so a blank field does not clear a date, it moves the record to now. And formatReleaseDateTime renders only to the minute, so a stored 16:27:56.919 re-parses to 16:27:00.000: editing a description would have quietly shifted a published patch note by 57 seconds. Measured against both real functions, not reasoned about. An untouched field therefore sends the stored ISO string, which chrono parses back to the identical instant; only a date somebody actually typed is re-read as prose; and a blank one is refused with the reason. Each image slot is its own op, so a slot nobody touched is never resubmitted — cachePatchImage re-hosts every URL it is handed, and re-sending an unchanged slot would upload five images to say nothing.

⚠️ The mockup's Season page keeps its own <style> block and the first adoption took only the shared sheet. 66 lines — the record panel, the masthead's create button, and two recorded fixes the mockup's own comments describe (.mtable .det must stay a table-cell; the ellipsis belongs on the box that actually overflows). Leaving them behind made every one of those classes an orphan-in-waiting, so the panel read as unbuildable when it was only unstyled. Adopted whole, same decision as app.css itself.

What the green suite could not see¶

⚠️ Three defects this session came from opening the page, and one from a probe that agreed with itself. The harness stub read URLSearchParams as a plain object, so the Bulk export ignored its mode: the button offered "All 125 MP builds" and the panel answered with 133 — one quantity, two authorities, disagreeing on screen while every test passed. Blanking a release date read "Nothing changed yet", the same words as an untouched form, while the real state was a refusal. And the batching helper used to apply these edits read every anchor from disk and deferred every write, which is right for N files and silently wrong for N edits to one: six of seven edits to armory.js were computed against the original bytes and overwritten by the seventh. One in-memory buffer per path fixes it; the write still happens once, after every assert.

⚠️ node --check accepted a duplicate top-level const again — a second SeasonRecord, colliding with the identity strip's own summary component. The build's ES-module parse caught it. Renamed PatchRecord, which is also the truer name.

Two forms in one realm spoke two different languages¶

The build editor is built from the adopted sheet's own sections; the add form was a row of bare inputs with display:flex;gap:8px written into the JSX — which is the exact shape this whole migration exists to remove. It is the mockup's bform now: sectioned, each field saying what its value MEANS, the derived weaponKey echoed live under the name that produces it, and a disabled button that says which kind of nothing it is waiting for.

🔴 It collected neither a gunsmith code nor a description, which put the portal behind Discord on a field Discord had to smuggle through a pipe-delimited convention because its modals cap at five inputs. A web form has no such cap; the omission was inherited rather than required. (Filed 2026-08-22; the editor half had quietly been done since, so the entry had gone stale on its own subject.) The share code field deliberately never blocks the button — correctGunsmithCode corrects a code rather than validating one, so a client-side validity test would refuse input the server would have fixed.

A blank share code sends no shareCode key at all, and that is asserted with a falsifier rather than merely followed: core/ops spreads the payload into a $set and an always-present '' wipes a real code. Nothing exists to wipe on an add — but a rule that holds in one op-builder and not the other has stopped being a rule.

⚠️ Every rank the form offers is now checked against the parser that reads it, because a dropdown producing a value the server silently discards is worse than no dropdown. The falsifier for that check had to be replaced: the first one used top9000close, which the real parser accepts — its pattern is top\d+, not a fixed list — so the throw came from the assertion's own wrong expectation rather than from anything being rejected. A vacuous pass wearing a falsifier's name is the one failure mode a falsifier exists to prevent.

The repairs panel the mockup specifies does not port, and the measurement is the finding¶

⚠️ fixMechanical was next on the list and was not built, because neither of its two rules is mechanical here. Measured against the real 133-build catalogue rather than reasoned about: rewriting an http image key to the WEAPON-N convention would hit exactly one build — the imgur-hosted row buildImageUrl passes through on purpose — and would point it at a Cloudinary key that may not exist, breaking a working image. The other rule, meta but unranked → top5, affects 2 records and is a guess dressed as a derivation, which the panel's own stated rule ("anything needing a judgement call is deliberately absent") excludes. And of the portal's five coverage flags, none has a derivable correct value: you cannot invent an attachment, and which of two duplicate builds to keep is what Compare is for. An affordance with nothing true to do is worse than an absent one — it implies the flags it sits under are fixable when they are not.

Three realms shipped an export button that ran, said nothing, and produced no file¶

🔴 window.open('data:text/plain;…') is blocked as a top-level navigation — measured in this app rather than assumed: the call returns null, throws nothing, and the page does not change. Season's, Armory's and Broadcast's Export selection all did exactly that. The third was found by a gate, not by hand: after fixing the first two, a source scan asserting nothing in portal/ui opens a data: URL immediately named Broadcast, which nobody had looked at. It ships with a falsifier.

⚠️ And Season's export was a caption, not a backup. It emitted title — window, which nothing reads back — so even if the navigation had worked, what came out was not restorable. The whole-list exports are the bot's own formatters now (formatDrawsAsBulkText, formatCalendarAsBulkText, formatPatchNotesAsText), and a selection writes real TSV. There is one download mechanism: the Blob-and-anchor path the changeset export has always used — the one export in this app known to work — extracted so a new one cannot reach for the broken kind by accident.

Export was reachable only by selecting rows first, so taking a backup of a whole season meant ticking every row of it, and retention rendered nowhere at all — which made "a copy is kept" a sentence in a dialog rather than something anybody could look at. The masthead carries an Export strip on every realm that has one: each scope with its record count, its own note, and a Kept this session list showing what was taken, when, how many rows and how many bytes, with the exact bytes handed back rather than a re-derivation.

🔴 Each scope states its own shape, because one line for all of them would be a lie. Draws and loadouts round-trip; the calendar is prefixed bullet lines; patch notes re-import through nothing at all, having no bulk-add flow, and the note says so. Telling somebody they hold a restorable backup of their patch notes is worse than offering no export.

⚠️ The mockup's empty state was NOT carried across. It reads "One-way operations stay locked until there is one" — false here, because the one-way strip deliberately does not gate on a session export; the interlock is the changeset export at Review, where it is real. The replacement says what the kept copies actually are (page-lived) and names where the durable one is. A test asserts the old sentence never comes back.

⚠️ A scopeless export is a refusal on both routes now, and the two test drivers that call every GET with a bare path share one map of which routes need a scope, rather than a copy each — a copy in the harness test would keep passing while the real route's contract moved, which is this branch's whole subject.

Two of this file's own gates were self-inflicted and worth recording. The data: scan flagged three files whose only offence was describing the defect in the comment that records it — a source gate that cannot tell code from prose fires hardest on the files that document the bug best, and trains the next person to delete the comment. And the scope-shape check matched up to the first }, which lands inside ${todayIso()} in a filename template, so every scope appeared to end three keys early.

The one irreversible operation in Season could not be inspected¶

🔴 A draft is built over weeks and promote replaces the live season with it — and nothing showed the difference. The scope switch let you edit the draft; there was no way to see what promoting it would actually do. That is the shape the whole staging model exists to remove, one level up: an action you cannot inspect before taking, and this one cannot be taken back. Compare sits in the draft bar, next to the thing it describes and above the strip that runs it.

On the harness's own fixture the answer turns out to matter: promoting blanks all three deadline titles and all three end dates, and drops the season from 37 items to 20. None of that was visible anywhere before.

⚠️ The comparison is on the stored DAY, never on the formatted string. A formatter renders one side Sep 10 and, given a value carrying a time, could render the other differently — so comparing display text reports a change where the record has none, which is a diff crying wolf on an irreversible operation. And TBD is a value, not an absence: a deadline moving from a real date to TBD is exactly what somebody needs to see, and comparing only the date fields would call that pair identical whenever both happened to be empty.

The composer's signature moment, and four probes that lied about it¶

🔴 The mockup names one thing /manage structurally cannot do: draw the item where it will land, before it is staged. Discord answers when with a line of text. The composer now reports what it currently describes and the Track draws it — dashed, in its own lane, at its own dates, with the lane it is aimed at tinted. A point is a diamond and a span is a bar, because a preview drawn in a shape the record cannot have teaches the wrong thing about the record.

⚠️ It reports the resolved ISO, never the typed text. aText is only what the field shows so a repaint does not discard half-typed words; a ghost placed from raw text would slide along the axis while somebody types "sep" on the way to "sep 21", and land on a day nobody chose. And a point's end is its start, whatever a stale second field holds — otherwise a draw draws as a bar.

The masthead's Add chips were dead once the composer was open. They call setShowAdd(key), which arrives as a prop, and useState(initialType) reads its argument once and ignores every later value — so pressing Playlist while composing a draw looked like a switch and did nothing. Found while probing for something else.

🔴 FOUR READINGS SAID THE COMPOSER COULD NEVER RESOLVE A DATE, AND THAT WAS THE PROBE, NOT THE CODE. The reason line read "That first date does not resolve to a day yet" and the Stage button stayed disabled — which reads as the composer's whole form path has never worked, and came within one commit of being written up as this branch's most serious defect. It was reading before the debounced round trip landed: the field waits 220ms, asks the server, and re-renders, and a read taken inside the same async function as the typing races that. Reading in a separate call showed "Ready to stage.", the resolved date under the field, and the ghost in the right lane. The same impatience explained two earlier "no ghost" readings, and a third came from setting three fields in one task — a pending re-render discards a value written to an input it is about to replace.

⚠️ A conservation check now covers the seam that made this invisible. The composer's type keys and the Track's lane keys are matched by string in two different files, and a mismatch fails silently: the ghost is computed, handed to the Track, matched against no lane, and never drawn. patchnote is the deliberate exception — the Track has no patch-note lane, so composing one draws nothing, which is honest rather than broken.

The Track drew three deadline lines and named none of them¶

🔴 .dend is a coloured hairline crossing every lane, and which colour meant which deadline was something you had to remember — while in the live season two of the three fall on the same day, so even the count was ambiguous. The rail is the flag row those lines were always missing: each deadline named, dated, tied to its line by a stem, in flow above the lanes so it takes its own height rather than sitting over them. A deadline outside the window is welded to the edge it is beyond with the distance in days, because "beyond this view" is a statement about the boundary.

⚠️ THE CHIPS DELIBERATELY DO NOT DRAG, and that is a decision rather than a reduced version of one. The adopted sheet gives .dflag an ew-resize cursor because the page it was drawn for had no other way to move a deadline. This portal has the identity editor directly above, where the date is typed and read by the bot's own chrono parser — and a season deadline has to land on an exact day, which a coarse gesture across a 44-day axis is the wrong instrument for. The cursor is overridden so the chip does not promise a gesture it does not have.

⚠️ Stacking is by proximity as a fraction of the visible span, not by measured pixel width. The mockup measures each chip's rendered width and re-stacks on every zoom; that needs the DOM and cannot be tested. Asking the same question of the data is approximate at the edges and deterministic — and a TBD deadline is neither flagged nor pinned, because drawing it at the date it used to hold would put a deadline on the axis the season has not set.

Twenty-six explanations were written and nothing could read them¶

🔴 data-tip is written across the Track's lane headers, its drag handles, the deadline rail and Review's rollback note — and the portal had no tooltip runtime at all. Every one of those sentences was markup nobody could reach. What hid it is the same thing that hid the async states and the tier-3 operations: .tip and .tip .sub are defined in the adopted stylesheet, and an orphan check asks whether a class has a rule. These had one. It was sitting unused.

A native title is not the same thing and is not the fix — it is OS chrome: delayed, unstyled, and rendered under the pointer, so it covers the thing it describes. The runtime is delegated from the document rather than bound per element, because the Track rebuilds its lanes on every zoom and drag: a per-element listener dies with the node, which fails intermittently, which reads as a fault rather than as a missing feature.

⚠️ The placement arithmetic is tested because it only fails at the edges — where a hand-check does not look. A tip prefers the right, flips left at the boundary, and clamps when it fits on neither side: a tip wider than the space either side of a centred mark runs off the left edge the moment it flips, and clamping only the right edge leaves that half of the failure in place. Two tips gained the second line the stylesheet's .sub row was written for.

🔴 A CROSS-FORMAT IMPORT PARSES CLEANLY AND BLANKS THE PAGE, and I made it while building this. Every *.logic.js loads as a classic script, so its functions are globals and there are no exports to name — import { tipPlacement } from './tips.logic.js' is valid module syntax, passes the build's own module-parse gate, and throws at load. season.js shipped the same mistake once before. scripts/buildPortal.js refuses the build on it now, with a falsifier.

⚠️ And that gate flagged three files whose only offence was describing the trap in the comment recording it — the SECOND source-scan gate today to fire on its own documentation. The data: URL scan did it first. Both strip comments before looking now, and the rule generalises: a source-shape gate that cannot tell code from prose punishes the files that explain the bug best, and teaches the next reader to delete the comment rather than keep the rule.

Three marks are drawn on every realm and none was explained¶

🔴 Solid is live, dashed is staged, hatched is a conflict. The Track's bars, the Board's cards, the composer's ghost and the Manifest's state pills all speak it — and a reader met it with no key anywhere in the portal. "Shape carries state" only works if somebody is told what the shapes mean once. The legend sits in the view bar, where the eye already goes and it costs no vertical space, and only on realms that actually draw the marks: a key for an absent mark teaches the reader the page is missing something.

🔴 AND THE ACCOUNT MENU ELIDED THE MIDDLE OF A DISCORD ID. The bar's chip shows the last four, which is fine as a chip — but the menu's Copy row showed nothing at all, and the mockup's own note says why the elision is wrong: the middle is the only part that distinguishes a snowflake from any other, so a preview that hides it cannot confirm the id is the right one, which is the entire reason anybody looks before pasting one into a grant. Nineteen digits fit. What you can reach became a note on the row it qualifies rather than a stat beside the session clock, and that row now goes to Access.

The Manifest gained its own label and a grouped chip set — the toolbar had a search box and loose chips with nothing naming the table they filter.

Access asked somebody to type a permission vocabulary from memory¶

🔴 Eleven scope tokens exist, manage silently covers eight of them, and the grant control was a comma-separated text box. A typo produced a grant that looked accepted and covered nothing — while the grid directly beside it renders every one of those tokens as a labelled, coloured cell. The vocabulary was on screen and unusable in the one control that needed it. The chips come from the same matrix.scopes the grid is built from, so there is no second list to drift, and the owner-only lock on destructive is shown rather than enforced here — the server decides that, and hiding it would leave an owner unable to grant the one permission only they can.

🔴 AND EVERY SESSION READ "LIVE", INCLUDING ONE LAST SEEN YESTERDAY. The row's state was the literal string 'live' for every session in the table. A browser session has no logout event unless somebody clicks one, so signed in now is derived or it is a guess — fifteen minutes is the ping window, because a tab left open keeps touching lastSeenAt and a closed one stops. A row with no timestamp now reads stale rather than live, which is the failure being replaced: a missing fact rendering as the reassuring answer.

⚠️ Sessions became a view and left the shared Manifest, which is where the hardcoded state came from. The Access mockup has no manifest at all. Two lists of one thing is the defect this branch has spent its life removing, and putting sessions in a generic table is what made "state" a column that had to be filled with something.

The single-point-of-failure mark had no legend. The underline is drawn on a column in the grid and flagged on a row in the by-scope view, and nothing said what it meant — a mark whose legend is missing is a mark the reader learns to ignore. It appears only when there is one.

Two panels on one screen were counting different rows¶

🔴 computeUsageStats has always excluded admin traffic. computeTimingStats never filtered it at all. So the Usage panel's counts and the Timing panel's percentiles — side by side, in Discord and in the portal — have been computed over different populations, with nothing saying so. /manage is the heaviest thing this bot does; a "usually 40ms" that silently includes it answers a question nobody asked. Found while threading a toggle through, not by looking for it.

⚠️ The fix deliberately does not move a shipped number. Making both exclude admin by default is the correct reading, but flipping it silently would change what /bot analytics has always printed — so the default is consistent and the Discord call sites override it explicitly. The discrepancy is now visible at the call site instead of hidden in a missing $match, and closing it is one argument away. (Worth a decision: whether /bot analytics's timing should keep counting /manage.)

The portal gets the toggle the mockup specifies — include admin traffic — and it re-asks the server rather than filtering in the browser, because there is no client-side subset of a p95.

Two blind spots in the instruments themselves¶

🔴 portal:orphans reads classes only out of class="…" and class=${…}, so a class passed as a DATA VALUE is invisible to it — and one shipped in this very session: metaClass: 'rowlife', a name with no rule in any stylesheet, not even the season page block folded in earlier today. The gate that exists to stop exactly that could not see it. It reads class-valued props now, and the unstyled class is gone rather than given a rule nobody designed.

⚠️ And portal:coverage was counting three phantoms nobody can ever emit. class="lvlb lv-${level}" scans as the literal lv-; so do t-${rank} and s-${kind}. A trailing-hyphen fragment is a prefix, not a class, and counting it capped the instrument's own ceiling below 100% for no reason. Dropped on both sides, so the mockup and the portal are measured by the same rule.

Both of these are the session's own subject turned on the tools: a gate is a claim about what it can see, and neither of these had been asked what it was blind to.

Eleven facts are written on every boot and two were read¶

🔴 models/BootRecord.js stores the commit, the host, the guild count, how many commands registered and how many emoji synced or went MISSING — and that last one is the known stale-prod-id trap, where a non-zero number means emoji render as raw ids in Discord. All of it was written on every boot and read by nothing. The Health panel showed the version and the kind. The card says what the missing count MEANS, not only how many, because a figure nobody can act on is a figure nobody reads. A conservation check ties every field to the model that declares it, so a rename there fails a test instead of rendering em-dashes forever.

And the river's level was a filter and never a mark — an error and a routine change read identically down the column, so the one thing you scan a log for needed the filter to be touched first.

⚠️ THIRD source-scan gate on this branch to fire on prose. The data: URL scan, the .logic.js import gate, and this one — which read the sentence "computeTimingStats() already returns the rows" as an unguarded call site. It is not coincidence: a file that documents a trap contains the trap's own shape in words, so a gate written without a comment-stripper fires hardest on the best-documented code and teaches the next reader to delete the comment. Strip first, always.

The table said what everything was CALLED and nothing about what is in it¶

🔴 A draw's whole point is the items it carries and their rarity. The row showed a title, a type and a date — so the one question a build or draw list exists to answer needed a click per row. The adopted table styles a detail cell, tier chips, a secondary line under a name and a right-aligned status column; all four were styled and none was emitted, and an orphan check could not see it because every one of them had a rule.

Season's rows now carry the rarity chips, the item names, whether the thumbnail is cached, a real window with its day count, and the lifecycle — not yet · running now · finished — under the type. Armory's carry the two-attachment peek with a +3, the gunsmith code (or DMZ — no code, which is a different fact from not set), and the badge chips, with the defect count as one chip naming the problems on hover rather than a comma-joined list of internal flag keys.

⚠️ Both ends of a lifecycle are inclusive. end < today retires an entry at midnight of the morning it is still live — which is the entire span of a one-day event, and eleven of this season's fourteen draws are single-day.

🔴 AND THE MANIFEST CALLED ITSELF "EVERYTHING IN THE SEASON" WHILE OMITTING THE DRAFT ENTIRELY — twenty items in the harness fixture, invisible in the one place that claims to list everything, so the only way to see what was staged for next season was to read it off the Track. Found because the NEXT SEASON mark keyed on row.isDraft and nothing ever set it: a branch that cannot be true is a button with no handler, one layer down. Draft rows join the table marked and staged, with a prefixed id — the Manifest keys rows, selections and the edit target on it, and nothing guarantees a draft subdocument's _id never matches a live one.

Compare showed two pictures where the record belonged¶

⚠️ .cmpcards expected .dcard children and got bare divs, so the column layout and every rule under .dcard.lc — twelve classes — styled nothing. The cards render the record now, laid out so two of them line up field for field: the attachment list is the thing you actually compare, and reading it out of two Discord renders means reading two pictures. The Discord render did not go away — it lives in the build editor's own side column, beside the fields that produce it, where it costs no request per picked build.

The instrument needed one more correction¶

portalCoverage's shared set mirrors the mockup's docs/superpowers/mockups/2026-08-23-portal-interactive/assets/shell.js — what every page shares — and Shell.Export is declared there, so every realm's want carries the export panel's vocabulary. Attributing the portal's exportPanel.js per realm made those classes read as missing from Door, which renders no realm surfaces at all and cannot be given one. Moving it lifts Door 70% → 78% and changes no markup. manifest.js and oneway.js deliberately stay per-realm: the mockup declares both in its shell too, but Home and Door render neither, and counting them shared would inflate exactly the realms this correction exists to stop mis-measuring.

Coverage 71% → 80% (Season 73% → 84%, Armory 61% → 76%, Broadcast 74% → 80%, Analytics 80% → 85%, Door 70% → 78%), orphans 0, and the round trip is demonstrated rather than asserted: exporting the fixture armory and pasting the result back reads as 2 update, 0 new.

Creation reached the masthead on every realm that has it, and the shortcut is written on the button. Measured on this branch: Armory's and Broadcast's only "new" affordance was a command-palette entry plus a button inside the Bulk view, and Access's grant form sat at the foot of a grid — the one thing an admin opens the portal to do was reachable only by already knowing where it was. Shell.MastheadNew is one control shared by all four, and it binds its own access key and renders it, from the same value, so the two cannot drift; the binding ignores the keystroke while a text field has focus, because a bare letter is a character before it is a shortcut. Access's button travels to the form and focuses the field rather than revealing a second copy — two grant forms can disagree, and one of them would be wrong.

The composer now says what it is about to create. It has drawn a ghost onto the Track since the Track was built, which answers where; nothing answered what, so a name typo and a mis-picked type were both invisible until after staging. The preview renders genuinely empty when there is nothing true to say, because the adopted sheet hides it with :empty and a "nothing yet" placeholder would reserve 76px of the composer forever.

Home stopped being unable to answer the portal's own question. The attention list says what is wrong and the clock says how long the season has; neither said what a player opening the bot this second would be shown. "Running right now" and "Showing to players" answer exactly that, and they re-use seasonItems rather than filtering again — Home has already been burned twice by holding its own copy of a predicate and disagreeing with the realm it links to. The staged-work strip offers the way back to Review and deliberately does not carry "Discard all": Review is the only screen that commits, and discarding everything from a summary strip that lists none of it is the one shape of that button nobody should press.

Access's scope grid says which scopes reach the portal at all. Eleven tokens, and whether one is a portal realm or Discord-only lived in a title attribute — a hover, on a row being read with the eyes. A scope with no holder besides the owner now reads "nobody but you" in quiet ink rather than sharing the warning colour with "single point": sole ownership is the resting state of a solo-maintained bot, and a mark that fires on the common case is a mark readers learn to skip. The permission drawer splits granting from revoking into groups coloured by direction — they had been two identical bold paragraphs describing opposite acts — and states the operation id the server will actually see.

Broadcast previews the message, not the records. It is the one realm whose output a player reads verbatim, and the accent colour, the delivery order and the embed cap were three separate facts on screen adding up to something shown nowhere. Anything past the cap is absent from the preview rather than greyed out, because a player does not see a faded row.

🔴 And a third instrument blind spot of the same shape, found by building work that was already done. portal:coverage extracted a dynamic class expression with [^}]* — which stops at the first }, and in class=${...} that brace belongs to the inner interpolation, not to the attribute. So lvtag scanned as the fragment ` lvtag lv-$ ` and both instruments reported it as unbuilt work that analytics.js` had been emitting since the river was written. Brace-matched now, and applied to the mockup and the portal by the same function — an asymmetric fix here is what inflated this instrument once already. Two of these were closed yesterday; a gate is a claim about what it can see, and a regex that cannot nest claims less than it appears to.

Three columns and a remove-column width stopped being decided in two places. A Manifest column may now name its own <col> class, which is what let the classifying column in four realms take the width the design gives it; and the remove column's width moved off th.ra onto .c-ra, so the colgroup's own stated rule — widths derive from a column's role — is finally true for every column rather than all-but-one.

🔴 AND THE NUMBER THAT WAS DRIVING ALL OF THIS TURNED OUT TO BE MEASURING TWO CODEBASES BY TWO DIFFERENT RULES. portal:coverage scoped the PORTAL by import graph — a realm is charged for oneway.js only if it imports it — and scoped the MOCKUP by FILE, so all 2,821 lines of docs/superpowers/mockups/2026-08-23-portal-interactive/assets/shell.js counted against every page. But that file is an object of members a page opts into by calling one: Shell.oneWay is called by season.html alone, Shell.compose by season.html alone, and door.html — a sign-in screen — calls exactly one member in the whole file. Seven realms were being charged for a one-way strip only Season mounts, and the Door for the composer's entire vocabulary. The partition is derived rather than listed: members are read out of the file, a call graph is built between them, and a page's shell vocabulary is the closure of what it calls. ⚠️ Both aliases — the pages use Shell. and S. interchangeably, and a scan for Shell. alone reported season.html calling 8 members when it calls 27.

Three more blind spots of one shape, in one instrument. ⓵ A dynamic class expression was extracted with [^}]*, which stops at the first } — and in class=${…} that brace belongs to the inner interpolation, so lvtag scanned as the fragment ` lvtag lv-$ ` and read as unbuilt work analytics.js had emitted since the river was written. ⓶ A class passed as a **data value** — a Manifest column's col: 'c-type', metaClass: 'rowlife' — never appears near a class= attribute, so Season emitted three and was reported missing all three. ⓷ A class computed into a **variable** (const kind = ci === 0 ? 'n' : … 'det' : 'ta-r') was the under-count this file's own header admitted to; it is closed, bounded by USE — only identifiers that actually appear in a class expression are resolved, so an unrelated const MESSAGES = […]` is never mistaken for a class list.

⚠️ One correction was made and REVERTED the same hour, and the reason is worth more than the change. Reading classList.toggle('is-slow', on) is the same rule applied to imperative code — and applying it charged the portal ~200 classes for a difference in mechanism, not design: the mockup is vanilla JS whose dominant way of expressing state IS a toggle, the portal is Preact whose dominant way is a computed string. The evidence that settled it is that the classes it demanded are ones the portal plainly implements — async.js emits is-refreshing and is-slow from a returned hostClass, the Track collapses lanes as lnc, and zero/stg-clear encode a rule shell.js deliberately reversed (a chip is absent at zero rather than dimmed). A measurement that moves because two codebases are written in different styles is measuring the style. The known cost is named rather than hidden: tips.js sets sub.className = 'sub' on the tooltip's second line, so sub reads as missing from all eight realms while the shared runtime has always emitted it.

**A new invariant ties the two gates together: a class the adopted sheet does not style cannot be wanted.** portal:orphans refuses a class with no rule, so an instrument demanding one was asking for markup the other gate forbids. It is a loophole if read alone — want now depends on a file this repo can edit — and it is stated as one: what closes it is that neither direction is free, since a rule with no markup is dead weight the stylesheet's own header calls out.

Coverage 85% → 96%, and UNBUILT went from 53 distinct classes to one. The one is fxc, unbuilt on purpose: a per-row opt-out in the bulk-paste diff would have to map a rendered row back to a block of raw text, and the parser that owns that mapping is the bot's utils/adminParser.js, which this codebase never reimplements in a browser. The textarea two inches away is the exact opt-out, and it is editable.

The last surfaces, in one pass. Season's Manifest draws each item's span against the same window the Track uses, with today marked on it; the Track shades everything past the last deadline (only a span can outlive a season, and the battle pass is rarely the latest of the three); its crosshair reads the date under the pointer and clicking it opens that day. Each deadline field says how long is left — the reason anyone opens that panel — and the rail marks dates where two deadlines coincide. Armory's bulk paste now says which fields an update overwrites, rather than the word "update" over a silent rewrite; the editor lists that build's own faults, on the one screen where they can be fixed. The Board's cards state both verbs instead of hiding "open" in a card click. The Manifest's checkbox is the design's drawn box rather than the browser's — the last UA-default control in the portal, on every row of every table — with the real input visually hidden so it keeps its focus and its keyboard behaviour. And the tray finally says the one thing that stops a commit.

.sr-only and .sr were the same rule declared twice, and the markup used the name the design does not. Consolidated onto the adopted sheet's .sr; the duplicate is deleted rather than aliased, because an alias is the duplicate with a comment on it. ⚠️ The test that caught it was itself wrong: it counted occurrences of class="sr-only", so a visually-hidden <span> counted as a label and a pure rename broke a check whose subject — every control has a label bound to it — had not changed. It asserts the association now.

🔴 AND THEN THE 96% WAS CHALLENGED, WHICH WAS RIGHT, AND THE REMAINING 4% TURNED OUT TO BE MOSTLY REAL. The claim was "built out" beside a number that said otherwise, and the split behind it — "three kinds, only one is work" — had been asserted after checking four of fifty entries. Enumerating all fifty with evidence produced a different answer: six of eight realms are now at exactly 100%, and what closed them was almost entirely surfaces, not measurement.

What was actually missing. The masthead's figures never moved — the sheet has drawn a rolling digit and a drifting +N badge since it was adopted, and staging a change updated a number silently, so the only signal your action landed was a digit you were not looking at. The scrubber marked its window with a 1px border instead of dimming everything outside it. A double-CP window — a real stored flag isDoubleCP, carried precisely so /draw calculator quotes the right price without anybody remembering an event is on — was drawn as an ordinary event bar, on the one screen showing the season's shape. Patch notes are dated season events and the Track drew none of them. Broadcast's post form was the last one still writing its layout into the JSX with its labels hidden — and those hidden labels carried the two facts that decide what the form does: a blank start means live on commit, a blank expiry means sixty days, not never. Armory and Broadcast could both stage work and neither could tell you it had any. A rejected edit landed in the tray, under the heading "Saved". And the Access grant form asked for a Discord ID and then the same ID again as a tier-3 confirmation, in two inputs that looked identical the moment either had text in it.

Three more instrument corrections, each with its boundary stated. A class-valued prop may be conditional (tone: staged ? 'stg' : undefined ships the class exactly as tone: 'stg' does). SHARED_UI is closed under imports the way the realm half always was — the Door has no entry module, so it was being measured against a shared set that stopped one hop short of the component that renders it. And a class expression's value may come from a helper: bandClass returns the literal 'bar saved', from a sibling classic script, so the base class of every bar on the Track was invisible. One hop, bounded to functions named in that initializer — following further would wander the module graph and start counting strings that never touch a class attribute.

🔴 THE INSTRUMENT ROUNDED A REGRESSION AWAY, AND ONLY FALSIFYING IT AGAINST ITSELF FOUND THAT. Deleting two live emitters from the Manifest is a real five-slot loss, and Math.round printed the result as 100% — the same headline a perfect score prints. The percentage floors now, and an exact 100% is reserved for have === want, so the top of the scale cannot lie. The footer states the two outstanding classes by name rather than leaving a reader to wonder what 99% is hiding.

Two classes remain unbuilt and both are decisions already on the record. addrow — Season replaced the mockup's inline add row with the inline composer above the Track, and restoring it would be a second way to add the same things with a different vocabulary and no natural-language dates. fxc — a per-row opt-out in the bulk-overwrite diff would have to map a rendered row back to a block of raw text, and the parser that owns that mapping is the bot's utils/adminParser.js, which this codebase never reimplements in a browser; the textarea beside it is the exact opt-out, and it is editable.

🔴 AND THEN A HARSH SELF-AUDIT FOUND SIX THINGS EVERY GREEN GATE HAD MISSED, INCLUDING ONE THIS SESSION SHIPPED ITSELF. The worst: the double-CP window could never render. It was written reading data.calendar, and data is the lane-keyed structure Season builds — draw/returning/event/playlist, with no calendar key — so the filter ran over an empty array and the window drew nothing, permanently, while portal:orphans saw a class with a rule and portal:coverage saw the class in the source. A class in a file is not a class on the page, and the metric this session spent itself raising is structurally incapable of telling the two apart. Also fixed: sev built as a headerless column of mostly-empty dots when the mockup puts it inside the name cell; a dead MastheadNew import; and five new logic functions shipped with comments describing their boundaries instead of tests enforcing them.

The dead branch now has the only kind of check that could have caught it. portalRender.test.js renders the real Track against a season carrying an isDoubleCP item and asserts a .win reaches the tree — proved by reinstating the bug and watching it fail, then reverting. Building it exposed a second defect in the harness itself: timeline.logic.js does module.exports = TL, so Object.assign(globalThis, mod) installed TL's members and never TL, and every component reading a bare TL — the entire Track — threw on render. Nobody had tried, so a broken harness read as "the Track has no render test". The global name is read out of the file's own window.X = line now rather than hardcoded.

🔴 AND A PIECE OF THIS SESSION'S OWN RECORDED REASONING WAS RETRACTED, WHICH MATTERS MORE THAN THE NUMBER. Earlier tonight a scan for imperative class writes was added, measured, and reverted with a confident comment: toggles are skipped because the mockup is vanilla JS and the portal is Preact, so reading them "measures the style, not the design" — argued from three examples off the top of a list of about thirty. Enumerating the tail refuted it: of the classes that scan surfaced, rolling, fdelta, errmsg, mark, ptc, stack, smask and nw-date-echo were eight real missing surfaces, every one of them subsequently built in this same release. The scan was right; the reasoning that dismissed it was a generalisation from a sample of three — the identical error, one hour apart, that produced the "built out at 96%" claim. The rule that actually survives is narrower and is now what the code implements: identity (.className = 'sub') is read; transient state (classList.toggle('is-slow', on)) is not.

⚠️ The framing of this release is worth stating plainly, because the number invites the wrong lesson. The story is not that coverage went 85% → 1493/1495. It is that a residual class list was used as a list of places nobody had looked, and roughly two-thirds of what it pointed at turned out to be real defects in a console someone relies on — creation reachable only from a command palette, a rejected edit rendering under the heading "Saved", two forms hiding the labels that carried their only surprising behaviour, a pricing-critical window drawn as an ordinary bar. The number is a side effect. Work that started from "what is this surface FOR" was consistently good; work that started from "which class is missing" was mixed — one design error, one probably-redundant panel, two unverified changes. A future session should walk the list and let it choose the QUESTION, never the answer.

⚠️ What was NOT done, said out loud: the page was never opened. Not once, in a repo whose own memory file says a green suite never means this is good. The harness exists, builds, has fixture flags and a live server, and npm test still does not open it — that is the structural gap, and it is filed rather than quietly dropped. OutcomeSplit in Analytics is probably redundant with the Usage panel's own ok/failed bars and is the one thing I would cut on a second look; Season's commit button and the composer's card preview are unverified and could be visual regressions.

🔴 A SECOND AUDIT, ASKED FOR AFTER THE FIRST ONE ENDED SATISFIED, FOUND SEVEN MORE — AND EVERY ONE WAS ABOUT SOMEBODY OTHER THAN ME. The first went deep on execution quality. The second changed frame, and that is the whole difference: the reviewer, the delegated admin, the keyboard user, the next session opening the file.

  • A class that styles nothing shipped to make a number move. tone: 'live' on Home's masthead — and there is no .stat.live rule anywhere (.stat.stg .v and .stat.warn .v exist). It counted because tone had been added to portal:coverage's prop list and not to portal:orphans', breaking the exact symmetry coverage's own header claims holds — "neither direction is free" — while it was false. The prop list is now one shared module both gates import, with a test asserting orphans reads it rather than keeping a copy that can drift.
  • Armory lost a keyboard affordance it had ninety minutes earlier. MastheadNew was built with an announced access key and a text-field guard; chasing mh-add/mh-t then replaced Armory's use of it with the mockup's bare chips — no key, no <kbd>, no guard — leaving two create idioms across three realms. The key binding is a hook now, and both chips carry theirs.
  • A stat lied to delegated admins. /api/review is forbidden to an admin without the review realm, so (review.ops || []) yielded [] and Armory's masthead read 0 staged when the honest answer is you cannot see that. A console whose entire permission model exists to separate those two rendered them identically. It reads an em dash now.
  • A comment justifying an accessibility decision became false and stayed in the file justifying it. The Track's crosshair was aria-hidden with the note "it says nothing a keyboard user is missing" — true when written, false the moment clicking it opened a day drawer that exists nowhere else. The drawer has a real keyboard path now (a focusable entrance, and previous/next-day stepping inside it), because the fix for a mouse-only affordance is a keyboard route, not a better sentence.
