Nameplate extraction never saw the bed, so its swatches came from unbacked translucent art. ⚠️ To be precise about the user-visible part: the panel was already surfacing the bed, appended as a fifth entry after the four extracted colours (2026-08-09). So nobody was missing that colour — what was wrong is that extraction spent all four of its slots on art it was reading without a backing, and the fifth entry tipped the page into a needless 1 / 2 pagination. Harkirat pointed out that Discord's static.png and asset.webm carry only the nameplate's upper layer; the background "bed" is a CSS gradient the client draws from the design's palette metadata. Measured against the real twilight asset before writing anything: static.png is 0.0% opaque (32.9% fully transparent, 67.1% partial alpha), confirming no bed is present in the bytes. Extraction was therefore reading translucent art with nothing behind it. A new renderNameplateExtractionMontage() pools evenly-spaced frames from the .webm, composites the gradient bed onto each, and tiles them into one still. On the real twilight/cobalt pairing the palette goes from #336CED #5B96F1 #1E4DE9 #83C5F4 to #0738C6 #1D56D6 #2E73DC #4D90E9 — the same hue family, but grounded in the bed the user actually sees rather than washed out by unbacked alpha.

⚠️ A claim in the first draft of this entry was WRONG and is corrected here rather than quietly edited away. It said the same art ships for every palette, so extraction returned an identical palette for lemon, crimson and clover, and that "a crimson nameplate reported blue". That cannot happen. A nameplate's art and its bed are a linked design — the palette is metadata describing which bed Discord renders for that design, not a free choice a user makes over arbitrary art (Harkirat, 2026-08-11 07:42 EDT). The three-palette comparison was a synthetic probe forcing twilight art onto beds it never ships with; it demonstrated that the code was bed-blind, which is real, but it was never evidence of a user-facing colour mismatch. The fix stands; the justification was overstated.

The four nameplate swatches are now one background plus three from the art, and there is no "Majority Color" among them. Harkirat's call: with only four slots a majority statistic doesn't earn one, and the background is a design fact rather than a measurement. Entry 0 is labelled "Nameplate Background" and carries the bed's hex exactly — nameplatePaletteHex already knows it, so extracting it from pixels could only approximate a value we hold precisely. The remaining three come from renderNameplateArtMontage(), which pools evenly-spaced .webm frames (art only, transparent backdrop) so a colour that appears part-way through the animation still counts; the caller over-asks by two and drops any art colour within MERGE_DELTA_E of the bed, so a near-duplicate never costs a slot. Measured on twilight: cobalt → #0131C2 + #2962E5 #4289E7 #1A2156, crimson → #900007 + three art blues, both with entry 0 exactly equal to the bed.

Designs whose palette is none already have their background baked into the art, so they get no prepended bed and take all four from the pooled art — nothing is invented.

Colour names stopped trying so hard, and the swatch labels followed them. Harkirat's read: names like "Rajah" and "Robin's Egg Blue" were straining for uniqueness. Naming now prefers the XKCD colour-survey vocabulary — crowdsourced from what ordinary people actually call colours — falling back to the old "Name That Color" list only when no plain name is close enough or the good one is already taken on that page. The nameplate bed outranks both and uses Discord's own palette word ("Cobalt", "Violet"). So Bunker, Yellow Sea, Pirate Gold became Almost Black, Yellowish Orange, Mustard Brown, and Japonica, Rajah became Dark Peach, Peach.

The labels were plained up in the same pass, since name and label are read together on one line and "Almost Black / Dark Undertone" mixed two registers: Majority Color → Most Common, Dark Undertone → Darkest Tone, Vibrant Accent → Boldest Color, Secondary Color → Second Most Common, Complementary Tone → Opposite Hue, Balanced Tone → Similar To Main. The rules that assign them are unchanged; only their wording is.

⚠️ The obvious version of this is a trap, and it was measured rather than assumed. Switching to the CSS colour names collapses palettes — 148 names cannot separate eight shades of one image: across 146 real swatches they produced 19 duplicate-name pairs affecting 12 of 22 images, one avatar reading "black" three times in eight slots, against the old list's 3. XKCD's ~900 names beat the incumbent on both axes: plainer and fewer collisions (1 duplicate pair corpus-wide). A wider library survey was run at Harkirat's request and rejected on fitness, not licensing — color-name-list (MIT) names these same colours "Eigengrau", "Dream Vapour", "Bacon Strips", "20000 Leagues Under the Sea".

⚠️ The list is VENDORED (22.5 KB), not a dependency, and that was measured too. color-name-lists ships all 36 vocabularies in one 2.05 MB JSON retaining 6.90 MB of heap. Harkirat asked whether just the one list could be pulled instead — it can — that package exposes each list as its own file, at 0.18 MB — but it still drags 8 transitive dependencies that this repo's rules require attributing and copyleft-auditing, for frozen 2010 survey data. Vendoring the cleaned list costs 22.5 KB and no dependency at all.

⚠️ A public survey spells things how people typed them, and 54 entries had to go or be corrected. 28 crude joke names ("shit brown", "diarrhea", "piss yellow") sitting squarely in the olive band a khaki avatar reaches, 11 with slashes, 2 uselessly vague — plus 13 spelling and language slips found by scanning the whole list rather than patching what surfaced: Liliac → Lilac, Purpleish → Purplish, Greyblue → Grey Blue, and the non-English Azul/Rosa dropped. One further fix came from a near-tie: #FEFEFE is visually white, but "Pale Grey" sat 0.3 RGB closer than "White" and won, so near-ties now go to the simplest name.

"White" and "Black" are now reserved for the exact values. They're the two names a reader takes literally, so a swatch that is merely near them reads as though the panel rounded off — and near-black is the common case, since extraction averages a whole dark region. #FFFFFF is "White"; #FEFEFE is "Basically White". #000000 is "Black"; #010101 is "Basically Black". Both forms can appear in the same palette without colliding.

⚠️ Harkirat caught a collision in the proposal before it shipped: a Violet bed alongside an art colour whose nearest name is also "violet" would have printed "Violet" twice. Names are assigned across the whole entry set in order, so Discord's authoritative name claims its word first and the art colour falls through to "Lilac".

⚠️ Still open, filed rather than fixed: Harkirat's observation that because the extractor is deterministic, nameplate and decoration palettes are pure functions of (asset, palette) and should be cached globally and permanently rather than per-user — the same key the WebP cache already uses.

Pre-Release v3.5.0

#112 8e0c794

Every command Dioreo can reference now becomes a real, clickable slash-command mention (</name:id>) instead of plain backtick text — click one and it types straight into your chat box, no more copy-typing /settings by hand. Harkirat found the format in Discord's own docs and tested it by hand first (a mention placed in the dev bot's own bio); the trickiest part isn't documented well: a subcommand or subcommand-group mention (/draw prices, /patch notes, /season end) still resolves off its TOP-LEVEL command's id — there is no separate id per subcommand, and a wrong one fails completely silently, rendering as plain text with no error.

IDs come free: index.js's existing command-registration call to Discord already returns every command's real id in its response, so client.commandIds is built straight off that with no extra API request. A new utils/commandMentions.js resolves the mention at render time, matching the convention utils/emojiMap.js already uses for emoji ids — a value that only exists after the bot is connected to Discord must never be frozen into a module-level constant, since the dev and prod bots are separate Discord applications with different ids for identically-named commands.

Landed in /help's landing directory and every detail page's command heading, plus six spots elsewhere in the bot where one command's text names a sibling command (/draw prices and /calendar's "check out /settings" tips, /server's two /settings mentions, /manage's /autobuild pointer, /autobuild's own retry/expiry messages, and /alerts' admin-only rejection). One genuine platform wall found along the way: a slash command's OPTION description (the grey helper text Discord shows while typing) is not message content and never renders markdown or mentions — /calendar's [view] option keeps its plain-text /settings reference for that reason, while the near-identical wording inside /help's own body (real message content) became a live mention. /help's Examples lines (option-value syntax, e.g. weapon:AK117) are intentionally untouched — a mention can't pre-fill an option value, and Harkirat parked that one for a later pass rather than a hard no.

Verified: boot-tested on the local dev bot; Harkirat confirmed /help's landing page, every detail page including the three subcommand cases, and all six cross-reference spots render as real clickable pills in Discord.

Pre-Release v3.4.2

#111 9a9244c

Every legacy v2 item now carries a verdict backed by code, not by the tracker. v2 closed barely an hour earlier, leaving docs/ROADMAP.md's three v2 batches as a queue nobody had reconciled — and the sweep's own filing warned that an un-struck item there meant unverified, not outstanding. Ten items, four buckets: 5 already done · 3 still genuinely open (re-tagged v3) · 2 folded into v3 by a prior decision · 0 abandoned. The empty bucket is written down on purpose so it reads as a checked conclusion rather than a step that got skipped. The useful finding is that shape itself — nothing in the queue had been overtaken or gone unwanted, so the cost of leaving it unread was never dead weight; it was three items whose true state nobody could read off the tracker.

The one real defect is the second sighting of a failure the repo already has a scar from. The pagination double round-trip perf fix sat un-struck and tagged [P2 · M] for four days after it shipped — adcec5a (#93) put the single-hop type: 7 UPDATE_MESSAGE into utils/sendV2Payload.js, and 138b25c (#97, v2.60.0) finished the job by deliberately reverting four routes over the blank-emoji bug. Its ⇄ twin in docs/db-deferred-list.md held that entire record the whole time. So the file answering "which version is this in" said open while the file answering "how big is it" said done — exactly the shape of the button-disable miss that prompted this sweep, where a struck-through line read as "done everywhere" while it had only ever shipped for /settings. Both times the reader got a confident wrong answer, which is the expensive part rather than the untidiness. The ⇄ marker records that a twin exists and nothing checks that the two sides still agree; a WARN-level docs-audit check for that is filed rather than built here, since it was outside the sweep's mandate.

Three items are genuinely open and now say why in code terms, so the next session does not re-derive them: View Colors' unset Display Name / Nameplate / Deco pages (getAvailableSources() still filters an unset source out entirely, so there is no button to hang a humor page on), the admin /status command (nothing built at all), and richer in-bot logging — which was half-shipped and had been readable as untouched. v2.41.0's utils/logger.js delivered the transport (structured severity plus service/version/commit); it never delivered the attribution the item is actually about, and its exports carry no component field. That narrows the remaining design question from "build a logging system" to "how does a component identifier get attached".

Three more records were corrected in passing, all the same failure family — two copies that only agree if a human compares them. Two [P1] hook-confirmation reminders sat nine lines apart under a byte-identical heading while being about different hooks: the notes hook is now confirmed firing (from this session's own startup context, the only place that evidence can come from), and the other was mis-titled, was really about completeness-sweep.sh, and had been answered three lines above it on 2026-08-06 12:35 EDT — it stayed open for four days directly below its own answer. Its three accepted design limits are preserved verbatim in the archive rather than lost with it. Separately, a verbatim duplicate reminder said "7" and "6" open notes items while the live figure was 8; collapsed, with the count removed rather than corrected, since a present-tense number in prose is a second source that can only rot.

The v5 section was a dumping ground, and Harkirat's correction to its framing exposed why. It had been headed "most speculative" — wrong, and actively harmful: "they're still very real plans", just experimental, not needed yet, or further up a step-ladder. But the deeper problem was that the section held three different KINDS of thing under one heading — far-future features, completed status notes from July, and a decided-no. A status note is not a work item and a decided-no is an answer; neither belongs on a roadmap, and both had sat there for weeks reading as outstanding work. Four maintenance items moved to a new version-neutral section (filing maintenance under a version number implied it was gated on v3 and v4 shipping first), the index.js split moved into v3, and six stale residents were swept to the archive — each verified first, and one of Harkirat's six calls was wrong in the useful direction: "Verify Cloudinary folder organization" is not stale, just a twenty-minute check that had been filed under a far-future heading, which is exactly why nobody ever picked it up.

Two pre-launch build items were promoted into v3, and the launch checklist gained a Step 0 because of them. The index.js split (P2 → P1; measured at 4,157 lines, not the "~3,313" on record — it grew 840 lines while parked in a queue justified by its size) and /draws + /calendar auto-expire (P2 → P1, scoped as one session for both commands). ⚠️ The ordering matters beyond bookkeeping: the split rewrites the interaction router that the checklist's step-1 click-test exercises, so click-testing first means doing it twice. docs-audit gained a triaged-exemption mechanism rather than a silenced warning. It is a genuine optional dev overlay (utils/emojiMap.js:120, read only under NODE_ENV=development, fail-soft). Pre-Release v3.4.0

#109 b85b6d2

The v3 guild install's launch blocker, closed. Shipping a guild-installable bot with no server-side controls means any member can invoke it in any channel with no moderator recourse — Harkirat's framing was "we don't want the bot to run freely bypassing everyone's oversight." /server is the answer: a Components V2 panel for a server's own admins, distinct from /manage, which stays Harkirat's owner-level surface gated on ALLOWED_ADMIN_ID. Design + the rejected alternatives: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-10-server-admin-visibility-policy-design.md.

"Blocked in a channel" means forced-ephemeral, not refused — and that reframe is what made the feature buildable. The bot is invited with permissions=0 and holds zero standing guild permissions, so it cannot delete a message, hide an invocation, or post outside the interaction that triggered it. The one thing it fully controls is its own response. Since it is slash-command-only, an ephemeral answer is a complete experience for the person who asked while being invisible to everyone else. So the feature is a response-visibility policy engine, not an access-control list, and naming it that in code stops a future session re-growing it into permissions the bot cannot back up. Harkirat also scratched "redirect" outright in the same pass: answering in a different channel needs a real channel permission on the invite link, which is a trust decision rather than a coding one. It is filed in docs/db-deferred-list.md alongside a config audit log and per-command role gating.

Six precedence tiers, and the four configurations that motivated them all express directly. Default visibility per server; channel rules; role rules that may be scoped to specific channels; and command rules that sit above both. Highest tier wins, a same-tier conflict resolves to public (mirroring Discord's own role-overwrite semantics, where an explicit allow beats a deny), and server admins bypass the command tier only — never the channel or role rules, which they set for the whole server including themselves. scripts/guildPolicy.test.js pins all nineteen cases and is wired into npm test; half of them exist purely to catch one tier silently reordering another.

The panel got rewritten for being unreadable, which was the right call. The first draft explained replace-semantics, the search affordance, thread inheritance and Discord's 25-per-menu cap as four stacked paragraphs on the Channels page — every sentence true, and a wall of text before an admin reached anything actionable. Harkirat: "this wall of text is just overwhelming at first glance." Every page is now a heading, one line of orientation, the current state, and at most one footnote. The detail moved to a new Server Admin category in /help, carrying the full precedence order, the intended default-then-exceptions workflow, and both Discord limits — framed as guidance rather than warnings, since a server that needs 25 role overrides wants a different default instead.

Answering a question about that cap found a silent defect. Harkirat asked what happens past 25 channels or roles. Those menus were never at risk — they are native type-8 and type-6 pickers that Discord renders with its own search over the whole server. But the command menu is a string select, capped at 25 options with no search, and it sliced the list bare. There are 18 gateable commands today, and the per-category weapon commands are generated from Loadout.distinct('category'), so the list grows: past 25, the extras would simply never appear and nothing would tell an admin the list was incomplete. It now names whatever it had to leave out.

/help now has two independent permission tiers, and shows each person only what they can actually run. Harkirat's structure: /server sits inside Preferences with an (Admin) suffix rather than in a section of its own — a whole heading for one command made the directory top-heavy for the handful of people who can see it — and Preferences swaps its emoji to ServerSettings and its description to "Manage your personal & server admin settings" when a server admin opens it. A new Bot Admin category lists /manage, /alerts and /autobuild, gated on the bot's own whitelist and absent entirely for everyone else; those had been deliberately excluded from /help altogether, which meant Harkirat could not look up his own commands.

/autobuild's private boolean became visibility (Hidden/Public), finishing a rename that had been described as bot-wide since v3.1.0. It was the last private left in the bot. The reason it survived is worth more than the fix: .claude/rules/commands-overview.md carries an explicit list of every renamed command, and /autobuild was simply not in it — so anyone checking coverage against that list got a clean answer. An enumeration that is quietly incomplete reads as complete, because the list is the verification. The list now names it, with a note to derive that claim from rg rather than trust the enumeration.

The Bot Admin and Preferences pages were rewritten after review. Every option is documented rather than just visibility — /manage's data_for with its eight sections, /autobuild's five. The shared visibility option is stated once per page instead of repeated under each command, matching the shape Gunsmiths already used. Preferences gained a real separator between /settings and /server (bodies can now request one, since a markdown rule inside a Text Display is a row of dashes, not a divider) and the /server section was cut roughly in half for being overwhelming. The whitelist explanation moved to a 💠 hint at the foot of the Bot Admin page — it explains the section rather than being something you do.

The two tiers are deliberately not a hierarchy. A server owner is not a bot admin, and Harkirat is a bot admin in servers where he holds no Manage Server — so visibility is a requires field naming which level a thing needs, checked against a { serverAdmin, botAdmin } object, rather than one boolean that would conflate them. requires on a category hides the whole section; requires on a command hides one line and leaves its category standing. Every surface reads the same fields — dropdown, landing directory, cmd: autocomplete and the detail bodies — so a restricted command is one entry and cannot be half-added. Both checks are free: computed permissions off the interaction payload, and an ID comparison. Anyone who reaches a restricted page through a stale dropdown gets the directory back rather than an error about a page they cannot see.

Adding that category walked into a pre-existing trap, so the trap was removed rather than documented. /help's dropdown and autocomplete map over CATEGORY_DEFS; its landing directory was five hardcoded lines. The new category appeared in the dropdown and was silently missing from the list. Harkirat, on being told: "that's a real gap that will create staleness and needs a proper solution." The directory is now generated from the same array, so a category is one entry and cannot be half-added — verified as a pure no-op by diffing the rendered container before and after, byte for byte. The half of the trap that survives is a category declared without a matching body builder, which would render undefined or throw when picked; a test now renders every declared category, and a negative control confirms it catches exactly that.

**A second test file covers whether the policy is ever applied, not just decided.** scripts/guildPolicy.test.js tests a pure function — the easy half, and it would pass unchanged while every rule silently failed to reach a message. scripts/guildPolicyEnforcement.test.js adds eighteen cases over the parts that actually enforce: the schema round-trip (an undeclared field is dropped on save, this repo's oldest recurring bug class), the ephemeral bit being OR-ed into the Components V2 flag rather than replacing it (replacing it renders a blank message, which would be debugged as a rendering bug), the clamp being own-enumerable so buildSyntheticInteraction() carries it through a navigation click, the "Show Everyone" strip, the truncation warning, and the 40-component ceiling on every page. None of it needs a database or a network, deliberately — a test that skips itself when Mongo is absent reports green while examining nothing, which is exactly what privacy-model-coverage did to this same feature.

Threads inherit their parent channel's rule, which was a real hole found by deriving angles rather than by any check. In a thread interaction.channelId is the thread's id, so a rule on #general matched nothing once conversation moved into a thread of #general and the answer posted publicly — failing open, in a feature whose whole job is to restrict, and threads are created continuously so an admin could never pre-empt them by listing each one. A rule on the thread itself still beats the inherited one, and channel-scoped role rules inherit identically. Nothing in this repo could have caught it: every other test case passes channelId as an opaque string and so cannot tell a thread id from a channel id. Five named cases now pin it, taking the suite to 19.

The policy is a ceiling, never a floor. An ephemeral verdict overrides both the visibility option and the saved UserPreference. A public verdict only permits a public answer — the user's own choice still decides. A server can quiet the bot; it can never make someone louder than they chose to be, and it can never read or change a personal preference.

A command rule forces ephemeral rather than removing the command, because removing it is not possible for a bot to do. Harkirat asked for the stronger version — take the command off the list in that server entirely. A bot cannot hide a global slash command inside one guild: guild-scoped registration does not delete global commands, Discord merges both sets, so omitting one leaves the global copy visible. The only native mechanism is application command permissions, which require an OAuth2 bearer token from a MANAGE_GUILD user; the bot cannot set them for itself. Admins already hold that lever directly in Server Settings → Integrations. The panel says so in plain words, because an admin will otherwise read the command's continued presence as a bug.

What Discord already covers natively — measured twice, and it retired this feature's justification twice. Both of these are settable per role and per channel: disabling Use Application Commands removes every slash command from every app, and disabling Use External Apps forces app output to ephemeral. So user-installed invocations were never ungoverned, which is what the roadmap entry had assumed. The fallback claim — that a guild-installed app is not "external", so that lever would stop applying in exactly the configuration v3 launches — was then tested and also proved false (2026-08-10 18:04 EDT, with a member who does not have the app user-installed, so the invocation came from the guild-installed copy; the permission forced it ephemeral anyway). Two gaps survive and are the entire justification for what shipped: the native lever is blunt, quieting every app in a channel where /server quiets this bot alone, and nothing native can force one command ephemeral while the rest stay public. The channel and role tiers therefore duplicate a native overwrite in shape, and deliberately mirror its semantics so admins' existing intuition transfers.

Enforcement lives at two choke points, and deliberately not in the commands. The obvious design — make resolveEphemeral() policy-aware and pass the policy in — was built and then removed: it is called by only nine commands (/help, /timestamp, /colors and the eight per-category weapon commands built dynamically in index.js never touch it), so it would have become an optional argument at nine sites where forgetting it looks identical to passing it. Instead attachGuildPolicy() wraps reply/deferReply/followUp on the interaction itself, and sendV2Payload() strips the "Show Everyone" row on the way out — that button posts a brand new genuinely public message, so leaving it live under an ephemeral rule is a one-click bypass. Same reasoning as utils/logger.js's patchConsole(): one patch that cannot be forgotten beats a rule that must be remembered.

/server is guild-channels-only, and it still follows you into servers where the bot is not installed. Harkirat caught it live: the command appears anywhere he goes, because it registers setIntegrationTypes([0, 1]) and a *user*-installed command travels with the user. setDefaultMemberPermissions(ManageGuild) cannot hide it either — Discord ignores that field for user-installed invocations, which is exactly why the runtime admin check is the real gate. Keeping [1] is deliberate: the policy applies to a user-installed invocation too, so registering [0] alone would create servers where the rules are active but unconfigurable. What could be fixed was fixed — setContexts([0]) removes it from DMs and group DMs, where it could only ever refuse.

The panel uses Harkirat's own ServerSettings emoji, and the comment beside it was wrong on the first draft. It claimed the id was dev-only and that uploading it to prod was a v3 launch blocker; a live read of /applications/@me/emojis against both applications showed it already existed in prod, so the literal is the prod id like every other entry and refreshEmojiIds() re-points it by name on the dev bot. The same read raised a question about Events and got the wrong answer out of it: prod still carries 1532830530108653659, the id emojiMap.js has always had, and since Discord mints a new id on every replacement, prod's copy was clearly never touched — from which this entry briefly concluded prod was still serving a broken emoji. Harkirat corrected it: prod's copy was always the correct one; the dev app held the broken copy, and that is the one he replaced. Both are right now, and nothing needs fixing. The mistake is the useful part — **an id proves whether an emoji was replaced, never whether it was *correct***, and the id comparison was quietly asked to answer a question about image content that it cannot reach. The evidence was real and the inference on top of it was not.

A privacy check reported a vacuous pass over the very model it exists to catch. GuildSettings.updatedBy stores a Discord user ID — personal data by the policy's own §2.1 reasoning — but docs-audit's privacy-model-coverage keys on the three literal names discordId/userId/user_id, so it never examined the new model and reported green. The heuristic now includes actor fields (updatedBy, createdBy, authorId, ownerId), which both closes the blind spot and clears a standing vacuous-pass warning: the audit went 39/41 → 40/41 verified. PRIVACY.md gained §2.1a and an Appendix A entry describing the record in full, folded into the pending v1.11 revision that ships with v3.

Pre-Release v3.3.0

#108 1dcf68a

The GIF cache shipped the same day, and got pivoted the same day. Commit 8b7ae18 (earlier today) added animated GIF previews for the Nameplate/Deco pages in View Colors. A live test — DMing the bot an attachment and asking Harkirat to check both desktop and mobile — confirmed Discord autoplays animated WebP inline exactly like GIF, and WebP holds real 8-bit alpha. That single fact removed every GIF-era compromise this feature had just shipped with: the solid-opaque nameplate bed (GIF's binary alpha genuinely couldn't hold a fade) is gone, restored to the real fade gradient; decoration's Bayer alpha-dithering (the closest a binary-alpha format can get to a soft edge) is gone entirely, replaced with true lossless transparency.

Discord's own external-media proxy turned out to be the harder problem, and it was chased down empirically, not assumed. A Components V2 media item referencing any external host — Cloudinary included — gets served through images-ext-N.discordapp.net, which re-encodes the image to lossy server-side before any client ever sees it. Measured directly: a real uploaded copy came back 2.2MB/lossy through the proxy vs. the 898KB/lossless original, same frame count and dimensions. Two workarounds were tested and ruled out with real data, not guesses: a quality=lossless-style query-string hint on the Cloudinary url (Discord mis-parses the appended query string as a literal path segment, breaking the reference outright) and substituting an external GIF for WebP (also gets reprocessed by the same proxy — this is general external-media behavior, not a WebP-specific quirk).

The fix: Discord's own cdn.discordapp.com is never proxied this way. utils/discordCdnStorage.js uploads each render once to a dedicated permanent server Harkirat set up specifically for this ("dioreoland"), with the bot invited there under real channel permissions — a deliberate, one-off exception to this bot's otherwise-absolute zero-standing-guild-permissions rule. The resulting CDN url is persisted in the Cloudinary resource's context metadata and preferred over the Cloudinary url on every future render — instant, no per-view network cost at all — with a fetch+reattach fallback (still lossless, just costs one round trip) for the rare case that url isn't available yet.

A genuinely nasty bug hid inside that fix for the first hour of live testing. Discord does not populate the classic message.attachments array for a file referenced only via attachment:// inside a Components V2 component — the resolved url lives only inside the component tree itself. uploadToStorageChannel read the wrong field, so the Discord CDN url was silently null from the very first render onward, and every fallback looked exactly like a race condition (an earlier fix that awaited the context-metadata patch, suspecting a timing bug, was reasonable but addressed a symptom that could never have mattered). Fixed with a generic recursive walk of the response's component tree rather than hardcoding indices.

Two real, measured performance fixes, found while live-testing with Harkirat: Cloudinary's Admin API lookup cost 138-470ms per call, even on a pure cache hit — added an in-memory memo so repeat views within the bot's process lifetime are instant. Decoration's per-frame Jimp loop was decode+re-encoding all 60 frames through Jimp even when the source (288×288) never once exceeded the resize cap — 736ms of pure waste, now skipped entirely when no resize is actually needed. img2webp's compression-effort setting (-m) turned out to be a pure size/speed tradeoff with zero quality difference at every setting (always lossless) — switched from the default to the fastest, since the storage-channel fix means these bytes now transfer exactly once per design, ever, making the ~14% size difference free.

Real nameplate design names, from a field Discord's own docs call unused. Discord's collectibles-shop REST endpoints are entirely blocked for bots (confirmed against four separate routes), and reverse-engineering the technique that already worked for palette colors turned out to be a dead end for item names — the full catalog is fetched live, not statically bundled. But the User API's Nameplate object carries a real label field ("COLLECTIBLES_NAMEPLATES_TWILIGHT_A11Y") that parses cleanly into the design's actual name, verified against two independent real nameplates. Decorations have no equivalent field and stay unnamed — Harkirat's call, after confirming there's genuinely nothing to parse there.

⚠️ Deploy blocker, not yet resolved: img2webp (separate from ffmpeg) is confirmed not installed on the production VM. Needs sudo apt-get install webp before or during the deploy that ships this.

Pre-Release v3.2.0

#106 4cf022c

The deferral was wrong, not the feature. .claude/rules/accent-and-colors.md had said since 2026-07-18 that per-server profiles needed guild membership and were "explicitly deferred to v4". The load-bearing half of that — "interaction.member is only reliably populated when invoked inside a guild the bot can resolve membership for" — was measured false. Discord sends the invoker's full server profile in the interaction payload of every guild, including ones the bot has never joined. The feature had been blocked for three weeks on a limitation that did not exist.

Colours now come from your server profile wherever you have one. Avatar, banner, decoration, nameplate and Display Name styles are all per-server, resolved independently — a server avatar with no server banner gives you the server avatar and your ordinary banner, which is exactly what Discord itself shows in that server. In a DM you get your global profile, because there is no server to read.

Measured across three real guilds and DMs, with different overrides set in each:

reachable when the bot isn't in the guildcost
avatar · banner · decoration · nameplate✅ in the interaction payloadfree
display-name styles✅ in the payloadfree
display-name styles, in a guild the bot has joined⚠️ needs a REST member fetchone call

That last row is the inversion worth remembering: discord.js's GuildMember._patch discards display_name_styles, so the case with more access is the one that costs a round trip — and the REST route it needs returns 404 Unknown Guild in the other case. Both paths are handled; whichever guild you're in, one of them works.

interaction.member arrives in three shapes and the difference is not cosmetic — a real GuildMember in a joined guild, raw JSON with no methods in one the bot hasn't joined (calling displayAvatarURL() there throws), and null in DMs. utils/guildProfile.js is the single normalizer; no call site branches on which.

Two bugs fell out that were never guild-specific:

  • A solid (single-colour) Display Name style was classified as "not set up" and silently fell back to avatar, because the check demanded colors.length >= 2. Global solid styles had been mishandled this way the entire time.
  • getCachedColor's avatar || 'default' hash is safe only for a User; a GuildMember would have collided every override-less member into one 'default' bucket that stops invalidating when their global avatar changes. Guild sources are routed so that can't happen, and the guard is now written down.

The cache is keyed on the image hash, deliberately NOT the guild id. Guild-keying looks obviously right and is wrong: the same server avatar reused across two guilds returns an identical hash, so hash-keying makes the second guild a free cache hit. Separate guild* field pairs exist only so a DM and a server don't evict each other's colours. No migration was needed — new fields start empty.

/settings shows your server avatar and banner (previews and both download buttons — they had to follow the same source, or the download would quietly hand back a different image than the thumbnail). /colors defaults to the same contextual rule, gains a from: override, and shows a Global ⇄ Server switch at the bottom — but only when you actually have a server profile there, since otherwise the two views are identical and the button would visibly do nothing. Asking for from:server where there is none explains why and offers to render your global colours instead.

⚠️ A profileSource setting was built and then removed (Harkirat: "let's just leave it honestly"). Which profile applies is decided by where you ran the command; a stored preference would only ever restate that. It is recorded in models/UserPreference.js as a "don't re-add this" note rather than silently vanishing.

Records: the "button emoji goes blank after a single-hop re-render" bug had been marked CLOSED since 2026-08-07 while still filed under "🐞 Active Bugs — broken behaviour, not yet fixed", and was absent from the archive — swept to docs/archive/resolved-list.md. The pagination-perf item still claimed "not yet click-tested live" when testing is precisely what forced four routes back to two-hop; it now says so.

Privacy: eighteen new cached colour fields, disclosed in Appendix A. The policy is deliberately staged as 1.11 (pending), dated "on the v3 release" rather than today — the site deploys only from main, so nothing publishes until v3 ships, and dating it in advance would have made a legal document claim an effective date that hadn't happened. Finalizing it is filed as a v3 launch blocker.

View Colors panel — four follow-ups from live-testing the above (Harkirat, same day): the panel now says which profile it's showing (> Extracted from: Server Profile / Global Profile) right in the heading, since colours resolve contextually with no stored preference and the switch is otherwise easy to miss. A solid Display Name style used to render Gradient Start/End/Blend as the same hex three times — it now shows the real colour once as Display Name Color plus two deterministic, same-hue companions, Lighter Tint and Darker Shade (gradients are unchanged). The Nameplate page finally composites the purple/red/green background bed behind the art — it lives in no asset Discord serves, only in the palette field the API already returned and this bot had been ignoring — and surfaces that bed colour as its own palette entry rather than baking it into the preview alone. The "Tap on the #HEX color code to copy it" hint moved from the heading to the top of the swatch list it actually describes.

Pre-Release v3.1.1

#105 a2b3840

A patch bump, deliberately (Harkirat's call, 2026-08-09 12:08 EDT). Guild install is landed but not finished — the per-server profile/colour work it unlocks is still queued, and the server-admin control surface is an open launch blocker. The 3.2.0-pre minor is being held until the colours implementation goes in, so the version reflects a partial feature rather than implying a complete one.

The whole session started as a two-line cosmetic bug and ended by moving a roadmap item forward a whole major version.

163cb1a had added client.user.setPresence({ activities: [...] }) to set the "Watching …" line under the bot's name. It didn't appear. **Three separate hypotheses were tested and falsified before the real one landed, and all three produced correct code that changed nothing:**

  1. Post-ready setPresence() was the bug. Plausible — presence is a documented IDENTIFY field, and discord.js otherwise identifies with its default empty presence: {}, publishing no status at all. Moved it into ClientOptions and verified it end-to-end down the wire (Client.js login() → options.ws.presence → WebSocketManager initialPresence → @discordjs/ws setting d.presence on the IDENTIFY payload). Still grey.
  2. A missing explicit status. Ruled out from the installed package source: ClientPresence.js already defaults status: data.status ?? 'online', so an explicit field was a literal no-op.
  3. An upstream patch would fix it. A GitHub issue prescribing exactly this fix turned out to be an open, unverified, AI-co-authored fork commit with zero comments — proposing, line for line, the change already made and already falsified.

The actual cause was never in this repo: presence is delivered only to users who share a guild with the app, and a user-install-only bot sits at guild_count: 0 — publishing correctly to an audience of nobody. Confirmed by controlled experiment on the dev bot: 0 guilds → grey dot, no activity card; joined one guild → both appeared instantly (propagates on GUILD_CREATE, no restart needed); kicked → both vanished; re-invited → both returned. Discord's own profile card names the mechanism, printing "1 Mutual Server".

That finding reshaped the roadmap. Guild install had been bundled into v4 alongside text/prefix commands and the privileged MESSAGE CONTENT intent. Those are separable — MESSAGE CONTENT exists for reading message text, which only prefix commands need — so guild install moves to v3 and takes on no Discord-approval dependency, while text/prefix commands stay v4.

What shipped here:

  • All 18 public commands now register setIntegrationTypes([0, 1]) — usable inside a server by people who have not user-installed the app. The 3 admin commands (/manage, /alerts, /autobuild) deliberately stay [1], since an admin command advertised in every server's command list is noise plus needless surface; each now carries a comment saying so, to stop a future session "fixing" the inconsistency.
  • ⚠️ 8 of those 18 were nearly missed. The per-weapon-category commands (ar/lmg/smg/sniper/marksman/shotgun/secondaries/all) are built dynamically in index.js, not in commands/*.js, so a sweep over that folder found 13 files and silently left the most-used surface in the bot behind. Caught only by reading back the live registration from Discord rather than trusting the source edit. A comment now marks that call site.
  • Presence lives in ClientOptions as BOT_PRESENCE, carrying a comment that records the confirmed finding and explicitly flags what is still untested — that guild membership, not the IDENTIFY move, is what the experiment isolated.

Measured on a real guild (permissions=0, no privileged intents), so the security posture is documented rather than assumed: reading the channel list ✅ · fetching a single member with roles ✅ · reading all 43 roles with permission bitfields and owner_id ✅ · enumerating members ⛔ 50001 (the privileged GUILD_MEMBERS intent — proven to be the intent and not a permission, since single-member fetch succeeds under the identical permission set) · acting on a channel outside an interaction ⛔ unchanged. No new data is stored, so the Privacy Policy is unaffected.

Documentation: root CLAUDE.md's "never a guild member" invariant was rewritten — the load-bearing half (zero standing guild permissions) survives intact and is now backed by measurements. ROADMAP split v3/v4 and gained a server-admin control surface item marked a launch blocker for guild install ([P1 · L · Opus5-High]) — shipping a guild-installable bot with no moderator oversight is how a bot gets mass-kicked.

Verified: node --check across all 13 command files + index.js · live command registration read back from Discord (18 × [0,1], 3 × [1]) · prod app confirmed untouched throughout at integration_types_config: ["1"], guild_count: 0 · docs-audit 39/41 (2 pre-existing, unrelated warnings) · docs:reflow 45 files, 0 changes.

Pre-Release v3.1.0

#104 b724a1e

The first real feature to ship on v3-pre-release. /help (ROADMAP.md's v3 list, filed 2026-07-15) went through three real passes in one session, each driven by direct feedback rather than a single upfront design.

Pass 1 followed the original design spec closely: five categories, static per-command blurbs, generic Unicode emoji. Harkirat's response was direct — "this design is so barebone... why does loadouts only have /dmz? what happened to /all? /ar? /lmg?" That caught a real gap: the per-weapon-category commands are generated dynamically at boot from live MongoDB categories (index.js's handleBotReady()), so a hardcoded list in /help would have gone stale the moment a category was added or removed. Fixed by querying Loadout.distinct('category', { mode: 'MP' }) at render time — one source of truth, not two that can drift.

Pass 2 rebuilt the whole thing from two real JSON mockups Harkirat sent — a landing page (mascot hero, Website/Install link buttons, a flat command directory) and a Gunsmiths detail page (a real Usage/Options/Examples structure). The mockup's own examples used visibility:\hidden\` as a value, which only makes sense as a string choice — confirmed directly rather than assumed, then executed as a **bot-wide rename**: hidden (boolean) → visibility (string choice, Hidden/Public) on every command with the option, not just loadouts (dmz/all/<category>/draws/draw prices/calendar/patch notes/season end/colors/settings/timestamp/manage/alerts). /patch notes' version option was also renamed to season`, with the autocomplete showing the real season title (e.g. "Season 6 — Take Your Heart").

Pass 3 polished wording end to end: dropdown descriptions rewritten to be genuinely useful instead of "sales pitch" phrasing, hint text de-duplicated against the landing page's own directory text, Options sub-headings restored under each split command, /timestamp got 5 example date formats plus a natural-language callout, and the "Made with love" footer became a real clickable mention (matching /settings' own existing signature) instead of plain text.

The best find of the session wasn't in /help at all. Two new emoji (DioreoCombo, Loadouts) rendered as broken text on the dev bot. A prior session had reported them already synced via scripts/syncMissingDevEmojis.js; my own first verification also (wrongly) reported them present. Both reports shared one root cause: a stale token, cached twice. The script authenticates from process.env.BOT_TOKEN and silently falls through to prod's .env if run without --env-file=.env.dev — since prod trivially matches itself by name, it reports "nothing missing" while the real dev app stays short. My own check hit the identical trap from a different angle: a reused sandbox process still had prod's token loaded from an earlier, unrelated Cloudinary upload, and dotenv's .config() never overrides an already-set variable. Forcing override: true and decoding both tokens' own embedded bot-user-IDs (rather than trusting a single API response) resolved it for real — re-ran the script correctly, uploaded the 3 missing emoji, verified 0 unmatched on boot. Filed to port the script into the dior CLI so the flag can't be forgotten structurally (/Applications/Claude Code/meta-deferred-list.md). Full story: docs/DEVLOG.md's 2026-08-08 22:36 EDT entry.

Documentation swept for staleness everywhere the rename and the shipped feature touch: ROADMAP.md (/help marked shipped, the Dev Portal listing reminder unblocked, 3 forward-looking hidden references in not-yet-built items corrected), db-deferred-list.md, .claude/rules/commands-overview.md (/help was missing from the command list entirely) and manage-panel.md, and docs/ideas/docs-system.md's own speculative "generate /help" idea flagged against the real, differently-built command that now exists. Historical records (past CHANGELOG entries, DEVLOG's own prior entries, the frozen pre-tidy notes archive) were deliberately left untouched — they correctly describe the past under the name that was current when written.

Verified: node --check across every touched file · scripts/checkEmojiCaptures.js clean (0 module-level emoji reads) · local dev bot boot-tested repeatedly through every pass, 0 unmatched emoji on the final boot · buildContainer() output hand-verified for every category state, all well under the 40-component cap · docs-audit 39/41 (2 pre-existing, unrelated warnings) · npm test 22/22 hook self-tests, 29/29 reflow checks, 0 hard-wrapped paragraphs.

v2.63.1

2026-08-09 23:55 EDT #107

A memory budget that was never measured, and two guards for the gaps prose kept missing

Internal workflow and enforcement only — no bot code is touched. All of it is fallout from an investigation into why perseus-vault, linksee and codebase-memory-mcp went unused despite standing "always use me" directives.

1. The MEMORY.md byte budget was never a measurement. The design spec chose 16,000 as "~20% above the post-consolidation target of ~9KB" — a number derived from another number. 20,000 was a reactive patch on 2026-08-08 after a session treated the self-imposed 16,000 as a hard wall and stalled on it. Harkirat settled it at 25,000, which is also the figure in Anthropic's own consolidate-memory skill, so the tool and the hook now agree instead of contradicting each other. There is no measured cliff near it: the old "24.4KB hard read limit" does not reproduce — a 33,530-byte memory file reads in full. Updated in every place carrying the stale number, and the tracker item whose premise this removes is re-tagged P2 → P3 and re-titled in the same edit rather than left for someone else.

⚠️ The lesson is about the number's provenance, not its value: a self-imposed constraint that nothing measured is the most expensive kind. It looks like rigour, so nobody re-tests it — and a later session then burns real time obeying an invention.

2. defer-in-place-guard.sh — the inverse of outstanding-not-filed.sh. That gate catches named but never filed; this catches an item that was filed — filed as someone else's job. A written-down deferral is otherwise indistinguishable from diligence and passes every existing check. Born from a real miss — writing a re-tagging instruction into an item that was already open for editing — and it caught its author within a minute of going live, on the registry entry documenting it. Scoped to new_string so the deferred-list's legitimate entries stay silent; self-exempt by basename, with a test pinning that a similarly-named file is still caught so the exemption cannot rot into a substring hole.

3. spec-handoff-coauthor-nudge.sh — cataloguing a tool is not adopting it. doc-coauthoring had been installed and available for a long time and used zero times. It was written into a memory file earlier in the same session and reported handled — but a reference entry is passive: it helps only a session that happens to open that file. Harkirat asked whether anything had actually changed to bring it to front of mind; one rg answered no. This fires at the one moment it matters — creating a new spec or handoff — and on new files only, so edits to an existing spec stay silent rather than decaying into noise.

4. The budget advisory now names its method. When MEMORY.md crosses the 90% line the hook points at consolidate-memory, notes both targets are the same 25,000, carries the one override that matters — its "retire dated files" step must not touch the feedback_* memories, which are durable by design and not re-derivable from the repo — and gives the path, since the skill lives outside ~/.claude and no search there reaches it.

5. scripts/devlog-add.mjs — the DEVLOG's two recurring failures made structurally impossible. Writing an entry by hand failed the same two ways on almost every release, and both were caught only by docs:audit after the bytes landed, so each cost an edit-and-recheck cycle: the entry appended at end-of-file landed after the # Part B marker (Part B is thematic; dated entries belong in Part A), and the Part A TOC went un-updated. Neither needs judgement — both insertion points are structural. devlog-toc and record-structure stay as the backstop and now name the script in their own failure messages.

⚠️ It writes from a subprocess, so it does not pass through the Edit/Write tools and triggers none of their hooks — which would have made it a net loss: one manual failure removed, three gates silently disabled. Harkirat asked directly whether it bypassed anything. It did, so it now runs them itself against the same payload the harness sends, reusing the hook scripts rather than reimplementing them — timestamp-check in both modes (pre denies an impossible stamp, post warns on a bare date), typos-check, and defer-in-place-guard. A missing hook is reported, never silently skipped. The pre-PR sweeps (records-close-check, stale-reference-sweep, completeness-sweep) were checked too and are unaffected: they fire on gh pr create and detect via git diff, so how the bytes were written is irrelevant.

Verification: 24/24 hook tests (the suite grew by exactly the two new hooks — coverage is computed from scripts on disk, so a missing test fails it), 16/16 and 12/12 for the new guards, 14/14 for memory-index-check, shellcheck clean, docs:audit 39/41 with no new errors. Both new hooks were fired live, not just pipe-tested — which is the entire lesson of the investigation that produced them: a pipe-test proves the script, never the hook.

v2.63.0

2026-08-08 12:05 EDT #103 2daaed4

Soft-wrapped prose, front matter on every doc, and a verified reflow tool

The documentation layer changed shape. Three asks landed together because they touch the same files: a hard-wrap policy decision, front matter across the docs, and the notes-scratchpad rework.

1. Prose is now soft-wrapped — one logical line per paragraph. Measured first, not assumed: 13,582 of 21,020 prose lines (64.6%) continued a sentence onto the next line, so most multi-word phrases physically did not exist on any single line and rg could not match them. Harkirat's call was to reflow everything now rather than let the old style age out.

⚠️ dior text unwrap was deliberately not used, and verifying that first is what saved the legal documents. Its flushQuote() collapses an N-line blockquote to a single >, destroying the bare > that separates quoted paragraphs — on docs/legal/TERMS.md it merged two distinct paragraphs and dropped the ## ⚠️ PLEASE READ BEFORE USING THE BOT heading into the body text. scripts/reflow-prose.mjs replaces it for this tree, verified at three independent levels: token conservation, structural counts (headings, table rows, HTML lines, quote breaks, list markers, byte-identical fences), and an independent CommonMark oracle (markdown-it, a new devDependency).

Three real defects were found by that verification rather than by reading, each now a regression test: /^\s*</ classed prose as HTML and tore …git show ⏎ <sha>:package.json… out of its paragraph; unindented lines were absorbed into list items, which CommonMark renders identically but which destroys an authored block boundary irreversibly; and the CLI ran on import, so a test importing verify() executed it and process.exit()ed before a single assertion ran while printing a confident "0 failed".

⚠️ The lesson worth keeping: render-equivalence is NECESSARY, NOT SUFFICIENT. TERMS.md and PRIVACY.md open with a metadata block that buildLegalPages.js reads one line per field. Joining it folded Version and Applies to into the rendered Effective value on the live site. CommonMark calls both forms identical, so the oracle passed it and every structural invariant passed it too — it was caught only by rebuilding the site and diffing public/. Any consumer that reads line structure is invisible to a general parser.

The memory store was reflowed too (85 files, same tool, same verification). It was named in the original deferred item's scope — "comments, memory, CHANGELOG/DEVLOG, docs" — and scoping it out silently would have split the convention across the two places a session reads most. MEMORY.md is unchanged at 16,212B, every file's front matter survived, and all 76 index links still resolve.

2. Every tracked doc declares kind: / status: front matter, enforced by a new doc-frontmatter (ERROR) audit check. kind is redundant with the folder at rest — its value is at MOVE time, turning a half-finished reorganization from a silent misfiling into a failing check, and making a file state its own tense contract when opened cold (frozen on a dated spec is the word that stops a session "helpfully" updating a snapshot). A published: true flag marks the 7 sources that render to dioreo.app, cross-checked against the generator's own page tables so the two cannot drift. description, updated, title and tags were considered and rejected: each would be duplicated state that rots, and git already knows the dates.

3. docs/ideas/diors-notes.md's preamble is a real section. The seven-comment HTML chain became prose under ## 📖 How this file works, and the lead-verb convention grew from 8 verbs to 17, grouped by what actually happened and ending with a decision procedure for the pairs that get confused (FIXED vs CORRECTED, IMPLEMENTED vs SHIPPED, ANSWERED vs VERIFIED, FILED vs DEFERRED, DEFERRED vs DECLINED). Two stale claims were fixed in passing: the preamble still sent readers to a section "at the very bottom of this file" and justified it by a hook scan range, both superseded on 2026-08-06.

4. The second-order fallout of changing wrap width, which Harkirat spotted from the diff itself (+6,184 / −20,300): every heuristic built on line counts silently became wrong. ~/.claude/hooks/usage-guard.mjs now thresholds its LARGE FULL READ warning on bytes rather than lines — verified, docs/ROADMAP.md (100 lines, 42KB) was silently under the old 400-line rule and warns correctly now. The two maintained docs/ideas/ files restated their prose volume in words (~337,000, wrap-invariant) instead of the now-meaningless "16,400 lines". And 19 notes L184-style breadcrumbs were rewritten to quote the item instead: 13 of 22 were already pointing past the end of the scratchpad, since a line number in a file that is constantly swept is stale by design. notes-line-refs (ERROR) prevents new ones; the append-only records keep their historical wording.

5. The completeness sweep stopped asking the same question every time. Harkirat's call — "too mechanical and restricted... like a train on tracks." Its pass 3 asked "which of my five registered angles has no signature in this session?", a question whose answer set is identical whether you rename a variable or reflow 44 files, so it could only ever catch pre-enumerated classes. Both real misses of this release were outside it. It now has three layers: the registry (cheap, deterministic), change-shaped demands computed from the diff (an item left a tracking list ⇒ account for every noun in its original scope · a bulk transform ⇒ name every heuristic that measured the property you changed · new enforcement ⇒ prove it can fail · a parsed file changed ⇒ run that parser before and after), and a required derivation run — Harkirat's idea — which the hook detects in the transcript and re-asks for twice before releasing. What makes it un-tickable: it demands at least one angle no automated check in the repo can see, plus an explicit list of what was not checked.

Also: memory-softwrap (WARN) — Harkirat again: "github ci can't check outside the repo, BUT WE CAN." My earlier claim that the memory store couldn't be covered was letting the weakest consumer set the bar; docs-audit runs locally before every PR. It reuses reflow-prose.mjs itself rather than a second heuristic, and skips loudly on CI. Its first version was written async while the runner calls checks synchronously — it verified nothing while reporting a pass, caught by reading the ledger's examined count rather than the verdict. And timestamp-check.sh's deny message now names its own escape tokens (TS-DEADLINE, TS-EXAMPLE): both existed, neither was mentioned, so a legitimate citation of a documented deadline was blocked twice and the message gave advice its own header calls wrong for scheduled events.

Also — outstanding-not-filed.sh gained TWO new shapes, both from live misses this session. Its existing tells all describe work being left behind, so two opposite-looking failures tripped nothing: (a) a promise to write a record ("I'll record it in memory") — caught when Harkirat asked "did you add the memory you stated?" and the answer was no; and (b) a decision parked inside a file — he asked directly whether soft-wrapping should extend to code comments, and the answer was written into CLAUDE.md as "an open question" with nothing said back to him. Both branches only read the final chat message, so a deferral written into a document was invisible, and the document even read as diligent because it named the gap. That question is now answered and filed with its measurement (6,193 of 10,174 comment lines, 60.9%, all 128 source files) plus the invariant that would make it safe.

GitHub Advanced Security's AI code review was disabled (Harkirat, 2026-08-08 13:32 EDT). Its github-advanced-security check failed on every push with CAPIError: 400 The requested model is not supported — GitHub's own service rejecting its own model request, with no workflow file and no model knob on our side (verified three ways). It never blocked a merge, since branch protection requires only syntax-check, but a permanent red badge trains everyone to read past failures. Full diagnosis preserved in docs/archive/resolved-list.md in case it is ever re-enabled.

CI hygiene, same release. The dependency audit is split by what actually ships: the production tree (--omit=dev, what the VM installs) is now a BLOCKING step and is clean at 0 vulnerabilities, while the dev tree stays visible and never blocks. Previously a single dev-inclusive audit printed a red "exit code 1" on every run under continue-on-error — a permanent red line inside a green build is how a real finding gets read past, and the net effect now is that a genuine production vulnerability fails CI where nothing did before. The one dev finding is xlsx/SheetJS, unfixable via npm (SheetJS left the registry) and absent from production. actions/checkout and actions/setup-node also went v4 → v7, retiring the "Node.js 20 is deprecated" warning.

Verified: 29/29 reflow tests · 44/44 files render identically under CommonMark, with the oracle proven able to detect six corruption classes · public/ byte-identical after a full site rebuild · docs-audit 37/39 exit 0 · 64/64 audit self-test proofs · outstanding-not-filed 19/19 · npm test 22/0 · notes hooks unchanged at 6 open items, and the follow-up hook proven still alive by running it against the pre-restructure file.

v2.62.1

2026-08-08 09:49 EDT #102 71d300f

Remediate 16 of 24 GitHub code-scanning alerts on the legal-site generator

GitHub Advanced Security opened 24 code-scanning alerts on 2026-08-06 across scripts/buildLegalPages.js, scripts/lib/chronicle.js, and both .github/workflows/*.yml files. Triaged individually rather than batched or dismissed wholesale — read each flagged function's full body and traced where the flagged string actually flows, not just the CodeQL summary text.

16 were real, fixed here. esc() (buildLegalPages.js) only escaped & < >, not quotes, despite being used inside double-quoted HTML attributes (meta content, data-lang, data-label, download) as well as text nodes — an unescaped " there could close an attribute early (js/incomplete-html-attribute-sanitization, 12 alerts). stripTags() (buildLegalPages.js) and labelOf() (chronicle.js) strip real tags from already-rendered HTML and re-embed the result unescaped — the CONTRIBUTORS page legend and the devlog's Lessons/TOC labels — so both now also escape any stray </> an imperfect strip regex missed, deliberately without touching & (the input is already-escaped, and re-escaping it would double-encode legitimate entities like &amp;) (js/incomplete-multi-character-sanitization, 2 more alerts). Both workflow YAML files gained an explicit permissions: contents: read — neither ever writes with GITHUB_TOKEN (actions/missing-workflow-permissions, 2 alerts). public/ was rebuilt and committed alongside — visually identical (&#39;/&quot; render the same as the literal characters), confirmed by the build's own 100%-content self-verifier plus a manual grep for double-escape artifacts across every published page.

8 were false positives, dismissed with documented reasoning rather than silenced — see docs/db-deferred-list.md → 🚫 Decided-no. All eight sit inside build-time audit/gate functions (structureAudit(), crossRefAudit(), scriptSyntaxAudit(), chronicle's heading classifiers) where the flagged string is only ever compared or .test()-ed against internally — it never reaches a page actually served to a reader.

A 9th false positive turned up from CodeQL's own re-scan of this PR, on the stripTags() fix itself: its dataflow model evaluates the tag-strip regex in isolation and doesn't credit the unconditional character-class escape immediately after it, even after matching the tool's own advisory-recommended fix shape exactly. Since that escape runs on every code path with no branch around it, no residual </> can survive — a provable false positive, suppressed inline with // lgtm[...] rather than chased through further rewrites. Also documented in docs/db-deferred-list.md.

Real-world exploitability was already low throughout (every source Markdown this generator renders is this repo's own — docs/legal/*.md, LICENSE, NOTICE, the three changelog records — never user-submitted), but the escaping gaps were genuine and the fix was free.

Fixing the hook that made v2.61.1 necessary

Harkirat asked directly why the release-doc-check hook flagged the missing design-decisions.md update only after v2.61.0 had already merged, forcing v2.61.1 to exist at all. Investigated rather than assumed: git log -S on both files confirmed the PostToolUse "RELEASE DOC CHECK" hook (checks origin/main, after gh pr merge) has run this exact check since 2026-07-28, five days before release-ready-check.sh (the PreToolUse, pre-merge equivalent) was built specifically to fix this class of wrong-moment bug. 2026-08-07 22:06 EDT #98 87ed7a5

/manage's calendar bulk add/replace now reports a per-category breakdown, not just a count. Harkirat bulk-added 23 calendar events with no manual category prefixes and several MP-mode/BR titles landed under Events instead of Playlists — the classifier itself turned out correct (an explicit e• prefix was present in the actual submitted text, not visible in what he'd retyped for review), but the confirmation message gave no way to catch it without opening /calendar and cross-checking by eye. /calendar page banners were silently going dead within ~24-48h, and the width-cap feature built to fix a desktop-width nuisance turned out to be a complete no-op anyway. The 2026-07-31 decision to skip Cloudinary re-hosting for Discord-CDN banner sources ("a real Discord CDN link doesn't expire") was built on a false premise — media.discordapp.net links are signed with expiring ex=/is=/hm= params; decoding a live one showed it had already expired. Two workarounds (height=auto, forging a later ex=) both failed on direct testing. Separately, the width cap itself (capBannerPreviewWidth) only ever sent ?width=N, which Discord's resize proxy silently ignores without an accompanying height — confirmed it had never actually resized anything. Fix: utils/calendarBannerCache.js now re-hosts every banner source to Cloudinary unconditionally (durable, no expiry), and the width cap was dropped entirely rather than fixed — Harkirat live-tested a working version and rejected it anyway, since a Cloudinary-transformed derivative has no path back to the original, so the cap also shrank the zoomed view. Banners now render at full resolution, inline and on zoom, from a durable host.

Every Cloudinary-hosted image in this bot now uses adaptive format/quality (f_auto,q_auto), not just loadout screenshots. Investigating the banner issue surfaced that draw thumbnails and patch-note images never applied this either — only loadout images (which build their delivery URL fresh at render time) did; the other three modules stored Cloudinary's secure_url verbatim, at full/original quality. New shared utils/cloudinaryDeliveryUrl.js (withDeliveryDefaults(), idempotent, non-Cloudinary URLs pass through untouched) is now applied on every upload/lookup across cloudinaryCache.js (draws), patchNotesCache.js, and calendarBannerCache.js — the standing convention going forward for any Cloudinary URL this bot produces. scripts/ backfillCloudinaryDeliveryDefaults.js (safe to re-run) fixed everything already stored on both dev and prod (25 URLs each), each spot-verified live.

The bug that looked fixed, and the fix that traded speed for correctness

2026-08-07 13:49 EDT #96 cee3180

A purge that looked like data loss, and wasn't

/manage calendar bulk add/replace could time out with no visible confirmation. The handler never called deferReply() before its DB fetch + parse + (replace-mode) fuzzy-match + save() — all inside Discord's 3-second interaction-ack window, unlike the sibling draws bulk handler a few lines up which already deferred. Once the window was blown, interaction.reply() failed on a dead token ("Dior's Builds didn't respond in time") even though the save had already gone through — so data landed with no confirmation, which is what made this look broken rather than just slow.

A real draw went missing from /calendar's Draws page after a calendar-events purge, and the data was never actually the problem. Traced end-to-end against the live production database (an earlier pass wrongly diagnosed this against the dev database instead — see DEVLOG): the draw was correctly in newDraws, correctly synthesized by getDrawSectionEntries(), and correctly deduped against an explicit calendar row. The actual bug was isEventEnded() treating a same-day-released draw as "ended" the instant its UTC-midnight release timestamp passed — for any US-timezone viewer, that's almost immediately. Combined with an Active-Only calendar filter preference, a draw released today would silently disappear from the filtered view within hours while /draws (no such filter) kept showing it fine. dateOnly entries now never count as "ended" — they only disappear when actually removed from newDraws/returningDraws, matching /draws' own behavior, until the already-queued season-expiry feature gets built on purpose. Also fixed: guessCalendarCategory()'s draw-keyword regex only matched the spelled-out "two", never the numeral a real title might use.

The Guide emoji wasn't broken code — the dev Discord application was just missing the asset. refreshEmojiIds() re-points an existing same-named emoji to whichever app is booting; it can't create one that was never uploaded. Confirmed directly against Discord's API (not assumed) that the dev app had 76 emojis and no "Guide." Synced via the existing scripts/syncMissingDevEmojis.js — a duplicate script was built first and caught before merge (see DEVLOG).

Two visual asks: /draw prices' region-switch buttons changed from red to blue; /calendar's three section-toggle buttons (Draws/Events/Gamemodes) now carry emoji.

New: an unconditional dev-bot duplicate-instance check at SessionStart. The existing guidance ("suspect multiple instances if the bot behaves erratically") was reactive and memory-dependent — it missed a real collision this session where repeated git switch calls restarted the --watch dev-bot child mid-session. The new hook distinguishes a normal --watch supervisor+child pair (same parent/child PID relationship) from a genuine second, independently-launched instance on the same token, and only speaks up for the latter.

v2.58.2

2026-08-07 11:22 EDT #93 ed0225f

A tolerance window, a round-trip cut, and a CI-only bug hiding in both

timestamp-check.sh's future-stamp gate went from a zero-tolerance string compare to an epoch-second compare with a 3-minute grace window. The old [ "$d $hm" \> "$now" ] check denied a perfectly honest write the moment ordinary turn latency (a minute or two between reading the clock and the bytes landing) put it a few minutes ahead of a stale $now. Still catches what the gate exists for — the original incident was stamps drifting 4.5 hours into the future — while no longer denying single-digit-minute drift from normal operation.

That fix's own date -j -f parse was BSD/macOS-only, and silently went dead on CI. ubuntu-latest runs GNU date, which rejects -j; the parse error was piped to /dev/null and treated as "unparseable, skip," so the whole future-stamp gate parsed nothing and denied nothing in CI — 46 of 47 test-suite assertions failed there while all 47 passed locally on the Mac dev machine, because the Mac path never exercised the failure branch. Found by reading a failed CI log, not by re-running the suite locally (which stayed green the entire time). Fixed with a BSD-first, GNU-fallback parse.

Draws/calendar/drawprices/settings pagination and settings toggles now cost ONE Discord round-trip instead of two. These paths are pure string-building — no image or network work before responding — so the deferUpdate() ack that used to run before every click bought nothing but latency. sendV2Payload() now POSTs directly to the interaction-callback endpoint as the first and only response when the interaction hasn't already been acked; any path that still defers first (the initial slash invocation, heavy paths like View Colors) is unaffected. One latent bug fixed while removing the settings toggle's deferUpdate(): it used to pass the real interaction straight through when actingUser === interaction.user, relying on that removed call to make settings.js's own deferral guard a no-op — now always synthetic with a no-op override, matching every other branch.

memory-index-check.sh's budget guard only ever warned once ALREADY over budget — a session reading its "ok" status at 98% full had no signal anything needed attention before the next line simply didn't fit. Added a 90%-threshold advisory tier, distinct from the hard over-budget error, with tests proving both fire independently.

Also: every docs/db-deferred-list.md item now carries a model+effort recommendation from the priority-tier grid (Harkirat's standing ask — a reference for whichever session picks it up, not a binding order), synced to the canonical copy of that legend in the cross-project tracker.
